laietani.t: The Iberian people of the coast around Barcelona, known later for the wines of Laietania and their coins minted at Barkeno.
laietani.o: The Laietani lived on the coastal plain and hills between the Llobregat and Tordera rivers, around modern Barcelona and the Maresme, from about the 5th century BCE. They formed part of the Iberian culture of the north-east and traded with Emporion and other Greek ports.
laietani.r: Their society was based on fortified hilltop towns such as Burriac and Puig Castellar, with grain storage silos and craft workshops. They minted coins with Iberian legends, including Laiesken and Barkeno. Under Rome their territory became famous for wine production, mentioned by Pliny and exported in amphorae across the western Mediterranean.
laietani.e: The Laietani were subdued during Cato's campaign of 195 BCE and absorbed into Hispania Citerior. Their hill towns were gradually abandoned for Roman foundations on the plain such as Baetulo, Iluro and, under Augustus, Barcino, the origin of Barcelona.

lordship-of-meath.t: The great Anglo-Norman liberty of Meath granted to Hugh de Lacy, centred on the castle of Trim.
lordship-of-meath.o: In 1172 Henry II granted the former Kingdom of Mide to Hugh de Lacy to balance Strongbow's power in Leinster. De Lacy built motte castles across the territory and began the great stone castle at Trim, which became the largest Norman castle in Ireland.
lordship-of-meath.r: Meath was a liberty with its own courts and officials. De Lacy settled English tenants, founded towns and abbeys and married a daughter of Ruaidri Ua Conchobair, the high king. He was killed at Durrow in 1186. His son Walter de Lacy recovered the lordship after a conflict with King John and held it until 1241.
lordship-of-meath.e: After Walter's death in 1241 the lordship was divided between his granddaughters, creating the liberties of Trim and Meath. Meath later formed the heart of the English Pale.

lordship-of-mann.t: The Isle of Man under English lords, above all the Stanley earls of Derby, who ruled it as 'Kings' and then 'Lords of Mann' for over three centuries.
lordship-of-mann.o: After the Treaty of Perth of 1266 Man passed to Scotland, but it changed hands repeatedly in the Anglo-Scottish wars. From 1333 Edward III granted it to William Montagu, later Earl of Salisbury, and English rule became permanent. In 1405 Henry IV granted the island to Sir John Stanley.
lordship-of-mann.r: The Stanleys styled themselves Kings of Mann until 1504 and then Lords of Mann. The island kept the Tynwald, its own laws and the Manx language. James Stanley, 7th Earl of Derby, held it for Charles I, and his wife, Charlotte de la Tremoille, defended it until 1651. Smuggling flourished in the 18th century because of low duties.
lordship-of-mann.e: The lordship passed to the Dukes of Atholl in 1736. To end smuggling, the British government bought the sovereign rights with the Revestment Act of 1765, creating the Crown Dependency of the Isle of Man.

lordship-of-argos-and-nauplia.t: Frankish lordship of the Argolid, held by the lords of Athens and their heirs, which ended when its last lady sold it to Venice in 1388.
lordship-of-argos-and-nauplia.o: After the death of Leo Sgouros, his last strongholds, Argos and Nauplia, fell to the Franks in 1212. The Principality of Achaea granted them to Otho de la Roche, lord of the Duchy of Athens, who held them as a fief of the prince.
lordship-of-argos-and-nauplia.r: For a century the lordship was held by the dukes of Athens, giving them a foothold in the Peloponnese and a port at Nauplia. When the Catalans conquered Athens in 1311, Argos and Nauplia stayed loyal to the Brienne heirs of Walter of Brienne and later passed to the Enghien family. Greek and Albanian farmers worked the fertile Argive plain.
lordship-of-argos-and-nauplia.e: Pressed by the Byzantines of the Despotate of the Morea and the Turks, the heiress Marie of Enghien sold the lordship to Venice in 1388. The Despot Theodore I seized Argos first, but Venice took control, creating Venetian Nauplia.

later-shu.t: The second independent kingdom of Sichuan in the tenth century, a prosperous haven of poetry, painting and learning under the Meng family.
later-shu.o: After the Later Tang conquered Former Shu in 925, Meng Zhixiang was appointed military governor at Chengdu. When the Later Tang court tried to rein him in, he resisted, absorbed neighbouring eastern Sichuan and in 934 proclaimed himself emperor of Shu, dying months later.
later-shu.r: His son Meng Chang reigned for over thirty years in peace. Sichuan prospered from rice, silk, salt and tea, and Chengdu's court became a cultural centre: the Huajian anthology of song lyrics was compiled there in 940, the bird and flower painter Huang Quan worked in the palace, and the Confucian classics were carved in stone.
later-shu.e: In 964 the Song Dynasty invaded, and within weeks Meng Chang surrendered in 965. He was taken to Kaifeng, where he died soon after. Heavy Song exactions in Sichuan later provoked rebellions there.

lordship-of-rostock.t: Short-lived Mecklenburg lordship of the Niklotid princes around the Hanseatic port of Rostock, which fell under Danish and then Mecklenburg rule.
lordship-of-rostock.o: When Prince Henry Borwin II of Mecklenburg died in 1226, his lands were divided among his sons in 1229. Henry Borwin III received the share around Rostock, a town that had received Lübeck law in 1218. He and his heirs ruled as lords of Rostock, one of four Mecklenburg branches alongside Mecklenburg, Werle and Parchim-Richenberg.
lordship-of-rostock.r: The lords were descendants of the Obotrite prince Niklot, ruling a land newly settled by German farmers and townspeople. Rostock itself grew fast as a Hanseatic port and gained wide self-government, often at odds with its lords. The territory was small and the lords were pressed by Denmark and their Mecklenburg cousins, and in 1300 Nicholas the Child placed himself under Danish protection.
lordship-of-rostock.e: After Nicholas the Child died without a son in 1314, the lordship passed under Danish control and then to Henry II of Mecklenburg, who secured it by 1323. Rostock remained part of Mecklenburg, while the city kept its Hanseatic autonomy.

lordship-of-tinos-and-mykonos.t: Island lordship of the Venetian Ghisi family in the Cyclades, which ended when the last Ghisi bequeathed Tinos and Mykonos to Venice in 1390.
lordship-of-tinos-and-mykonos.o: The brothers Andrea and Geremia Ghisi, Venetian nobles, conquered Tinos and Mykonos around 1207 in the wave of private Venetian ventures that followed the Fourth Crusade. They also acquired other small islands, including parts of the Northern Sporades, and recognised the suzerainty of the Latin Empire and Venice.
lordship-of-tinos-and-mykonos.r: The Ghisi held the islands as a hereditary family domain, ruling from the hilltop castle of Exobourgo on Tinos over Greek farmers and fishermen, and were drawn into the feudal politics of the Triarchy of Negroponte and the Principality of Achaea. Byzantine raids under Licario in the 1270s cost them some islands.
lordship-of-tinos-and-mykonos.e: Turkish raids grew in the 14th century. Giorgio III Ghisi, the last of the line, died in 1390 and left his islands to Venice, which ruled Tinos until 1715 as Venetian Tinos.

latin-empire.t: Crusader state founded in Constantinople after the Fourth Crusade sacked the city in 1204, a weak empire that lasted fifty-seven years.
latin-empire.o: The Fourth Crusade, diverted by Venetian interests and Byzantine politics, stormed Constantinople in April 1204 and plundered it. The crusaders elected Baldwin of Flanders emperor and divided the Byzantine lands: one quarter to the emperor, the rest split between Venice and the crusader barons, who received fiefs across Thrace, Macedonia and Greece.
latin-empire.r: The emperors ruled with Western feudal institutions, while Venice controlled a share of Constantinople and its trade. A Latin patriarch replaced the Orthodox one, alienating the Greek population. Baldwin I was captured by the Bulgarian tsar Kaloyan at Adrianople in 1205. His brother Henry of Flanders proved an able ruler, but after him the empire shrank to little more than the capital.
latin-empire.e: Baldwin II pawned relics, including the Crown of Thorns sold to Louis IX, and even his son to raise money. In July 1261 troops of the Empire of Nicaea entered Constantinople, Baldwin fled, and the Byzantine Empire was restored.

lemovices.t: Gallic people of the Limousin who sent ten thousand men to relieve Alesia and whose name survives in Limoges.
lemovices.o: The Lemovices held the granite uplands of the western Massif Central, in the modern Limousin. Caesar lists them among the allies of Vercingetorix.
lemovices.r: Their land was rich in gold, which was mined in many small workings before the Roman conquest. Their main oppidum was at Villejoubert, near Saint-Denis-des-Murs.
lemovices.e: In 52 BCE they sent ten thousand men to Alesia, and their leader Sedullus was killed there. Under Rome their capital was Augustoritum, later Lemovices, from which come Limoges and the Limousin.

lupaca-kingdom.t: An Aymara kingdom on the western shore of Lake Titicaca whose vast llama herds and valley colonies made it one of the richest highland realms.
lupaca-kingdom.o: After the collapse of Tiwanaku, Aymara-speaking groups formed several kingdoms around Lake Titicaca. The Lupaca, or Lupaqa, emerged by the 12th century on the southwestern shore of the lake in present-day Peru, with Chucuito as their capital, and became rivals of the Colla Kingdom to the north.
lupaca-kingdom.r: The Lupaca kingdom had two paramount lords, reflecting the Andean division into upper and lower halves, and was divided into seven provinces. Its wealth lay in vast herds of llamas and alpacas. The Lupaca controlled colonies in the warm Pacific valleys of Moquegua and Sama, where they grew maize and cotton, a pattern called the vertical archipelago. Fortified hilltop towns called pukaras reflect frequent warfare.
lupaca-kingdom.e: The Lupaca under their lord Cari defeated the Colla around 1450 and allied with the Inca ruler Viracocha Inca. They were absorbed into the Inca Empire under Pachacuti. A Spanish inspection of Chucuito in 1567 by Garci Diez de San Miguel is a major source on their society.

landgraviate-of-hesse-rheinfels.t: A short-lived Hessian landgraviate on the middle Rhine, ruled by Philip II from Rheinfels castle above St. Goar.
landgraviate-of-hesse-rheinfels.o: In the 1567 division of the Landgraviate of Hesse among the sons of Philip the Magnanimous, the third son, Philip II, received the Lower County of Katzenelnbogen on the Rhine, with Rheinfels castle above St. Goar as his residence.
landgraviate-of-hesse-rheinfels.r: Philip II rebuilt Rheinfels as a Renaissance residence and fortress, controlling the Rhine tolls at St. Goar that were the territory's main income. His small state was Lutheran, like its Hessian neighbours. He married Anna Elisabeth of the Palatinate but had no children.
landgraviate-of-hesse-rheinfels.e: When Philip II died in 1583, his lands were divided among his brothers, most going to the Landgraviate of Hesse-Kassel, with smaller shares to Hesse-Marburg and Hesse-Darmstadt. Rheinfels became one of the largest castles on the Rhine before French troops blew it up in 1797.

lordship-of-imola-and-forli.t: A short-lived papal-nephew state in Romagna, famous for the defiant Caterina Sforza, who held out against Cesare Borgia.
lordship-of-imola-and-forli.o: In 1473 Pope Sixtus IV acquired Imola for his nephew Girolamo Riario, who married Caterina Sforza, daughter of Galeazzo Maria Sforza of the Duchy of Milan. In 1480 the pope added Forlì after the end of the Lordship of Forli.
lordship-of-imola-and-forli.r: Girolamo ruled harshly and taxed heavily, and was involved in the Pazzi conspiracy against the Medici in 1478. He was murdered in 1488 by the Orsi family; Caterina held the fortress of Ravaldino, saved the state and governed as regent for her son Ottaviano Riario, crushing her enemies. She dealt with Florence and Milan as an equal and became a celebrated figure.
lordship-of-imola-and-forli.e: Cesare Borgia attacked in late 1499. Imola fell quickly, and in January 1500 Caterina was captured at Ravaldino after a fierce defence. Both towns became part of Cesare's Duchy of Romagna.

lato.t: Dorian hill city of eastern Crete with one of the best-preserved Greek town centres on the island, home of Alexander's admiral Nearchus.
lato.o: Lato stood in a saddle between two hills above the Gulf of Mirabello in eastern Crete. Founded by Dorian Greeks, it was a city by the 7th century BCE, named after the goddess Leto, whose image appears on its coins.
lato.r: Lato's remains include an agora, a prytaneion, a temple and stepped theatral area, showing the civic life of a Cretan polis with kosmoi magistrates. Nearchus, Alexander the Great's admiral, came from Lato. Inscriptions record its wars and treaties with neighbours such as Olous and Hierapytna.
lato.e: Lato's harbour, Lato pros Kamara, grew in importance in the Hellenistic period. After the Roman conquest of 67 BCE the hill town declined and the coastal settlement became the main centre, forerunner of modern Agios Nikolaos.

ligures.t: Ancient peoples of the north-western Mediterranean coast and Alps, from the Arno to the Rhône, who resisted Rome in their mountains for nearly two centuries.
ligures.o: The Ligures were among the oldest recorded peoples of north-western Italy and southern Gaul, already named by Greek writers of the 6th century BCE as living around Massalia and the Gulf of Genoa. Their origins are obscure; their language survives only in place names and personal names, and its relationship to Celtic and other Indo-European languages is debated.
ligures.r: They lived as separate tribes, among them the Ingauni, Intimilii, Apuani and Statielli, in hill forts and upland villages, combining herding, small-scale farming and raiding. Classical authors described them as hardy and poor. They served as mercenaries for Carthage, and along the coast they traded with Greek Massalia and the Etruscans, while inland groups mixed with Celtic neighbours.
ligures.e: Rome fought the Ligures from 238 BCE onward, deporting thousands of Apuani to Samnium in 180 BCE. The last Alpine groups were subdued under Augustus, whose Trophy at La Turbie (7–6 BCE) lists conquered tribes. The region became Augustus's Regio IX, Liguria, a name that survives in the modern Italian region.

lyttos.t: Inland city of central Crete claiming Spartan descent, destroyed by Knossos in the Lyttian War of 220 BCE.
lyttos.o: Lyttos lay on a high plateau of central Crete, south-east of Knossos, and was one of the oldest cities on the island; it appears in Homer. Its people claimed to be colonists from Sparta, and ancient writers saw its customs as close to Spartan ones.
lyttos.r: Aristotle cites Lyttos as an example of the Cretan constitution with kosmoi, a council of elders and common messes. It controlled harbours on the north coast, including Chersonesos. Lyttos was a staunch enemy of Knossos and fought it repeatedly for leadership of central Crete.
lyttos.e: In the Lyttian War of 220 BCE Knossian forces destroyed Lyttos while its army was away. The city was rebuilt and resisted Rome until Metellus took it during the conquest of 69 to 67 BCE. It continued as a Roman town.

lordship-of-sligo.t: The lordship of the O'Connor Sligo, a branch of the royal O'Connors of Connacht, who ruled northern Connacht from Sligo Castle.
lordship-of-sligo.o: The O'Connors of Connacht divided after 1384 into O'Connor Don, O'Connor Roe and O'Connor Sligo. The Sligo branch, descended from Brian Luighnech, controlled Lower Connacht, centred on the town and castle of Sligo.
lordship-of-sligo.r: O'Connor Sligo ruled over lesser lords such as the O'Haras, O'Dowds and MacDonaghs, frequently contesting the area with the O'Donnells of the Kingdom of Tir Chonaill, who often claimed overlordship of Sligo. The town held a Dominican friary and was a busy harbour.
lordship-of-sligo.e: Under the Composition of Connacht in 1585, Sir Donal O'Connor Sligo accepted English tenure. The family's power waned, and their estates were largely lost after the 17th century wars.

lubavians.t: Small Prussian territory around Lubawa on the border with Masovia, given to the first missionary bishop of Prussia in 1216.
lubavians.o: The land of Lubawa lay in the south-west of Prussia, next to the Chełmno land and Masovia. Its people were Prussians, related to the neighbouring Pomesanians and Sasins, and lived in scattered settlements around strongholds.
lubavians.r: Little is recorded of them. Exposed to Polish influence, some of their leaders accepted Christianity: in 1216 Prussian nobles granted the land of Lubawa to Christian, the Cistercian missionary bishop of Prussia, making it one of the first mission territories.
lubavians.e: The area passed under the Teutonic Order during its conquest of Prussia in the 1230s and was assigned to the Bishopric of Culm, whose bishops resided at Löbau (Lubawa). The Prussian population merged with German and Polish settlers.

lordship-of-beirut.t: A Crusader lordship whose Ibelin lords led the barons of Outremer against Emperor Frederick II.
lordship-of-beirut.o: Baldwin I took Beirut in May 1110 with Genoese and Pisan ships, and the city became a lordship of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, first held by Fulk of Guines and later by the Brisebarre family.
lordship-of-beirut.r: Beirut was lost to Saladin in 1187 and regained by German crusaders in 1197. Its most famous lord, John of Ibelin, the Old Lord of Beirut, rebuilt the citadel and a palace whose marble and mosaics impressed visitors, and led the baronial resistance to the imperial officials of Frederick II in the 1230s. The city traded with Damascus and Cyprus, and its lords held lands on both shores.
lordship-of-beirut.e: After the Ibelin line ended, Beirut passed through heiresses. Following the fall of Acre in 1291, its garrison surrendered to the Mamluks in July and the city was dismantled.
ru: John of Ibelin, the Old Lord of Beirut

lordship-of-jerba.t: A Catalan and Sicilian lordship over the Tunisian island of Jerba, held by Christian admirals for half a century until a local revolt.
lordship-of-jerba.o: In 1284, during the War of the Sicilian Vespers, the admiral Roger of Lauria, serving the Crown of Aragon and Sicily, seized Jerba from the Hafsid Sultanate, together with the Kerkennah islands. The pope recognised Lauria's lordship, and he fortified the island with the castle known as the Castello.
lordship-of-jerba.r: A small Christian garrison held the castle while the Ibadi Muslim islanders paid tribute and kept their own law and religion. Revolts were frequent. After the Lauria heirs' rule faltered, the island passed to the Kingdom of Sicily, and the chronicler Ramon Muntaner governed it from 1311 to about 1315, describing his rule in his Chronicle.
lordship-of-jerba.e: A revolt of the islanders, backed by the Hafsids, overwhelmed the garrison in 1335 and restored Hafsid rule. Jerba remained contested between Spain, the Ottomans and Tunis into the 16th century.

lutician-federation.t: A pagan Slavic alliance east of the Elbe that destroyed German rule in 983 and was governed by assemblies and the oracle of the god at Rethra.
lutician-federation.o: The Lutici, or Veleti, were West Slavic tribes between the Elbe and the Oder, among them the Redarii, Tollensians, Circipanians and Kessinians. In 983 they rose against German rule, destroying the bishoprics of Havelberg and Brandenburg and expelling the margraves of the Northern March in the Great Slav Rising.
lutician-federation.r: The federation had no prince; decisions were taken by assemblies of the tribes, and Thietmar of Merseburg describes the temple of Radegast (Svarożic) at Rethra, whose priests consulted oracles. Remarkably, Emperor Henry II allied with the pagan Lutici against the Christian Polish ruler Bolesław I, causing scandal among churchmen.
lutician-federation.e: Internal war among the tribes in 1057 weakened the federation, and in 1068 Bishop Burchard of Halberstadt destroyed Rethra. The Wendish Crusade of 1147 and campaigns of the Duchy of Pomerania, Albert the Bear and Henry the Lion absorbed the Lutician lands by the mid 12th century.

liang-liang-shidu.t: A rebel state on the Ordos frontier founded during the collapse of Sui, which survived as a client of the Eastern Turks until 628, the last regime to resist the Tang.
liang-liang-shidu.o: Liang Shidu, a local officer in Shuofang commandery on the northern bend of the Yellow River, killed the Sui governor in 617 and proclaimed himself emperor of Liang. To survive he accepted vassal status and a title from the Eastern Turkic Khaganate, whose cavalry protected him.
liang-liang-shidu.r: Little is recorded of its administration. It held a thinly populated frontier zone of steppe and farmland and served the Turks as a base for raids into the Tang heartland. Its dependence on the khaganate meant its fortunes rose and fell with Turkish power.
liang-liang-shidu.e: When the Eastern Turkic Khaganate weakened in the late 620s, Tang armies besieged Shuofang in 628. Liang Shidu was killed by his cousin Liang Luoren, who surrendered the city, completing the Tang reunification of China two years before the Turkish khaganate itself fell.

lemko-rusyn-republic.t: A small Rusyn republic in the Carpathian foothills, proclaimed by the Lemkos in 1918 and suppressed by Poland in 1920.
lemko-rusyn-republic.o: After the collapse of Austria-Hungary, the Lemkos, an East Slavic highland people of western Galicia, held a council at Florynka in December 1918. Led by pro-Russian leaders, they refused to join either Poland or the West Ukrainian People's Republic and proclaimed their own republic, with Yaroslav Kachmarchyk as president.
lemko-rusyn-republic.r: The republic had a small council and local administration among Lemko villages but no real army or economy of its own. Its leaders hoped for union with Russia or with the Rusyns of Czechoslovakia and sent delegates to the Paris Peace Conference, without success.
lemko-rusyn-republic.e: Polish authorities tolerated the republic for a time but ended it in March 1920, arresting its leaders. The region became part of the Second Polish Republic, and most Lemkos were later deported during the Second World War and after it.

lusones.t: A Celtiberian people of the upper Tagus and Jalón, among the first to fight Rome in the Celtiberian wars of the early 2nd century BCE.
lusones.o: The Lusones lived on the high plateau around the sources of the Tagus and the Jalón, between modern Guadalajara and Zaragoza. Appian and Strabo count them among the Celtiberians, and they emerged in the later Iron Age.
lusones.r: Little is known of their society beyond their hillfort settlements and herding economy on the cold uplands. They appear in Roman narratives mainly as a source of fighting men in the wars of the 2nd century BCE.
lusones.e: In 181 BCE they took part in the First Celtiberian War, which ended with the treaty of Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus in 179 BCE. They were drawn into the later wars that ended with Numantia in 133 BCE and were then absorbed into Hispania Citerior.

lakz.t: A medieval Lezgian principality in southern Dagestan, known mainly from Arab geographers, that guarded the mountain hinterland of Derbent.
lakz.o: Lakz is known chiefly from Arab writers of the 10th century such as al-Masudi, who describe a numerous and warlike people in the mountains west of Derbent, generally identified with the ancestors of the Lezgins. When and how it arose is not recorded; it appears as a principality by the 8th or 9th century.
lakz.r: Al-Masudi reports that the people of Lakz lived in fortified villages, some still pagan, some Muslim, under their own rulers. The land lay in the Samur valley and neighbouring mountains, with farming and herding. The Shirvanshah State claimed it and its rulers bore the additional title Layzanshah.
lakz.e: In the 11th century Lakz was drawn into the wars of the Shirvanshahs and the Emirate of Derbent and then overrun by Seljuk raids. It disappears from the sources, though the Lezgin communities of its valleys remained.

later-liang.t: The first of the Five Dynasties, founded by the former rebel Zhu Wen when he ended the Tang in 907, with its capital at Kaifeng.
later-liang.o: Zhu Wen, a lieutenant of Huang Chao, defected to the Tang in 882 and was made governor at Bianzhou (Kaifeng). Over two decades he became the strongest warlord in northern China, took control of the court, killed Emperor Zhaozong in 904 and in 907 forced the last Tang emperor to abdicate, founding the Liang dynasty.
later-liang.r: Later Liang held the central plains along the Yellow River and made Kaifeng, at the head of the canal system, its capital, a choice later dynasties followed. Its rule rested on a professional army, but it never subdued its rival Jin (Five Dynasties) at Taiyuan and lost a major battle at Bochao in 911. Many regional rulers in the south accepted its titles while governing independently.
later-liang.e: Zhu Wen was murdered by his son Zhu Yougui in 912, who was overthrown by his brother Zhu Youzhen in 913. Jin steadily took Hebei, and in 923 Li Cunxu, now ruler of the Later Tang, captured Kaifeng; Zhu Youzhen had himself killed.

lima-culture.t: A culture of the central coast of Peru whose adobe pyramids and irrigation canals laid the foundations of settlement in the valleys where Lima now stands.
lima-culture.o: The Lima culture took shape around 100 CE in the Chillón, Rímac and Lurín valleys of Peru's central coast. Communities built canals that turned the desert valleys into farmland and began raising large adobe platform mounds.
lima-culture.r: Its main centre was the Maranga complex in the Rímac valley, with large mounds such as Huaca San Marcos, while Huaca Pucllana in modern Miraflores was built of small handmade adobe bricks set like books on a shelf. Society was organised around ceremonial centres led by local elites. The economy combined irrigation farming with fishing. Pottery shows an interlocking serpent and fish design. The early phase of Pachacamac in the Lurín valley also belongs to this culture.
lima-culture.e: From around 650 CE the Lima culture declined as the Wari Empire extended its influence along the coast. Pachacamac continued as a sacred site and later became the centre of Ychsma. Many Lima mounds survive among the modern city's streets.

lordship-of-ireland.t: The territory in Ireland held by English kings as lords of Ireland from Henry II's invasion of 1171 until Henry VIII took the title of king in 1542.
lordship-of-ireland.o: Henry II landed at Waterford in 1171 to control Strongbow and other Norman adventurers. Irish kings and bishops submitted to him, and the papacy endorsed his claim. In 1177 he made his son John Lord of Ireland, a title merged with the English crown when John became king.
lordship-of-ireland.r: The lordship was governed from Dublin by a justiciar or lord deputy, with an Irish Parliament from the 13th century, English common law and shires. Norman lords built castles and towns, but from the 14th century Gaelic recovery and the Black Death shrank English rule to the Pale around Dublin, and the Statutes of Kilkenny of 1366 sought to stop settlers adopting Irish ways.
lordship-of-ireland.e: In 1541 the Irish Parliament declared Henry VIII King of Ireland, creating the Kingdom of Ireland in 1542.

landgraviate-of-klettgau.t: A small landgraviate on the upper Rhine between the Black Forest and Schaffhausen, ruled by the counts of Sulz and then the Schwarzenbergs.
landgraviate-of-klettgau.o: The Klettgau, a fertile district north of the Rhine near Schaffhausen, had been held as a landgraviate by the counts of Habsburg-Laufenburg. In 1408 it passed by marriage to the counts of Sulz, who ruled it from Tiengen.
landgraviate-of-klettgau.r: The counts of Sulz were also hereditary judges of the imperial court at Rottweil. Klettgau's peasants joined the Peasants' War of 1525 and were defeated. Losses to Zürich and Schaffhausen reduced the territory, and when the Sulz line died out in 1687 it passed by marriage to the Principality of Schwarzenberg, whose princes ruled it from afar through officials. It remained Catholic.
landgraviate-of-klettgau.e: In 1806 Klettgau was mediatised and placed under the Grand Duchy of Baden, which later bought out the Schwarzenbergs' remaining rights. The district now lies mainly in Baden-Württemberg, with its southern part in the Swiss canton of Schaffhausen.

latin-league.t: Alliance of the Latin towns around Rome, bound by shared cults and rights, that fought and then partnered Rome until Rome dissolved it in 338 BCE.
latin-league.o: The Latin peoples of the plain south of the Tiber shared a language, the cult of Jupiter Latiaris on the Alban Mount and other common sanctuaries from the early Iron Age. By the 6th century BCE they met in council at the grove of Ferentina and dedicated a federal shrine of Diana at Aricia, whose founding a Latin dictator, Egerius Baebius of Tusculum, is said to have led.
latin-league.r: The League was a loose association of towns such as Tusculum, Aricia, Lanuvium, Tibur and Praeneste, sometimes led by an elected dictator. Members shared rights of trade and intermarriage with each other. After Rome defeated the Latins at Lake Regillus around 496 BCE, the treaty of Spurius Cassius in 493 BCE made Rome and the League equal partners in defence, and they jointly founded colonies against the Aequi and Volsci.
latin-league.e: As Rome came to dominate the alliance, the Latins revolted in the Latin War of 340–338 BCE. Rome won, dissolved the League in 338 BCE and made separate treaties with each town. The shared 'Latin rights' survived as a legal status Rome later granted to colonies and provinces.

lampsacus.t: Phocaean colony on the Hellespont, famed for its wine and the cult of Priapus, where Epicurus taught and Anaxagoras died.
lampsacus.o: Lampsacus was founded by Phocaea c. 654 BCE on the Asian shore of the Hellespont, on a site said to have been offered by a local king. Its fertile hinterland produced wine that became the city's main export.
lampsacus.r: In the late 6th century BCE the tyrant Hippoclus and his son Aeantides ruled Lampsacus under Persia; Aeantides married a daughter of Hippias of Athens. Artaxerxes I granted the exiled Themistocles the city's revenues for wine. Lampsacus paid large tribute in the Delian League. Anaxagoras spent his last years there, and Epicurus taught in the city before moving to Athens.
lampsacus.e: Lampsacus appealed to Rome against Antiochus III in 196 BCE and became an ally. It passed into the Roman province of Asia in 129 BCE. The modern town of Lapseki stands on the site.

latin-archbishopric-of-patras.t: Church-ruled state in the north-western Peloponnese, where the Latin archbishops of Patras governed the city as secular lords for over 150 years.
latin-archbishopric-of-patras.o: The Latin archbishop of Patras was the senior Catholic churchman of the Principality of Achaea. Around 1276 the archbishops acquired the rights of the Barony of Patras, giving them lordship over the city and its land in addition to their spiritual role.
latin-archbishopric-of-patras.r: The archbishops governed with the help of canons and knights, while acting as vassals of the princes of Achaea and increasingly as independent rulers under papal protection. Patras traded silk and currants with Italy. To defend themselves from the Turks and Byzantines, the archbishops placed the city under Venetian administration from 1408 to 1413.
latin-archbishopric-of-patras.e: In 1429 Constantine Palaiologos, future last Byzantine emperor, took Patras from Archbishop Pandolfo Malatesta's officials, and the citadel surrendered in 1430. Patras joined the Despotate of the Morea until the Ottoman conquest of 1460.

lower-yafa-sultanate.t: The sultanate of the Afifi family over the lower Yafa highlands north-east of Aden, a small British-protected state until 1967.
lower-yafa-sultanate.o: The Yafa tribes of the mountains north-east of Aden threw off the authority of the Qasimid State in the early 18th century. The confederation split into an upper and a lower part, and the Afifi family established the Lower Yafa sultanate, with its seat at Al Qara.
lower-yafa-sultanate.r: The sultan was more an arbiter among tribes than a ruler with an administration. The region's terraced highlands produced coffee and grain, and Yafa'i men were known as mercenaries, serving the sultans of Hadramawt and the Nizam of Hyderabad. Lower Yafa signed a protection treaty with Britain and became part of the Aden Protectorate, joining the Federation of Arab Emirates of the South.
lower-yafa-sultanate.e: It was a member of the Federation of South Arabia until 1967, when the National Liberation Front took over and the territory was absorbed into South Yemen.

lordship-of-jever.t: A small Frisian lordship on the North Sea coast, remembered for its last native ruler, Lady Mary, and later held by Catherine the Great.
lordship-of-jever.o: Jeverland was part of the free Frisian lands of Östringen, Rüstringen and Wangerland, where local chieftains (hovetlinge) rose to power in the 14th century. Edo Wiemken the Elder, active from about 1359, built Jever into a lordship, and his descendants resisted the ambitions of the Cirksena rulers of the County of East Frisia.
lordship-of-jever.r: Mary of Jever, who ruled from 1517 to 1575, defended her small land against East Frisia by placing it under Habsburg protection as a fief of Brabant. She extended the castle, granted Jever town rights in 1536 and introduced the Reformation. The economy rested on cattle farming on the fertile coastal marshes. Childless, she bequeathed Jever to the County of Oldenburg.
lordship-of-jever.e: Jever passed to Oldenburg in 1575, in 1667 to Anhalt-Zerbst, and in 1793 to Catherine the Great of Russia, a Zerbst princess. After Dutch and French occupation it was transferred to the Duchy of Oldenburg in 1818. Jever's castle and brewery remain its landmarks.

later-jin-936-947.t: The third of the Five Dynasties, founded with Khitan help at the price of the Sixteen Prefectures, a loss that shaped China's northern frontier for four centuries.
later-jin-936-947.o: Shi Jingtang, a Shatuo general and son-in-law of Emperor Mingzong of the Later Tang, rebelled at Taiyuan in 936. He won the support of the Khitan emperor Yelü Deguang of the Liao dynasty by promising him the Sixteen Prefectures around modern Beijing and Datong, and with Khitan troops overthrew the Later Tang.
later-jin-936-947.r: Shi Jingtang called himself 'son' of the Khitan emperor and paid annual tribute, which shamed many officials. He moved the capital to Kaifeng. The cession gave the Liao the passes through the mountains north of the plain, leaving later Chinese dynasties exposed.
later-jin-936-947.e: His nephew Shi Chonggui, who succeeded in 942, refused to remain a vassal. The Khitan invaded repeatedly and took Kaifeng at the start of 947, deporting him to Manchuria. Liu Zhiyuan, governor at Taiyuan, then founded the Later Han.

lycian-league.t: The Lycian League, a federation of Lycian cities with weighted voting, praised by Strabo and cited by the framers of the US Constitution.
lycian-league.o: After the Romans freed Lycia from Rhodian rule in 168 BCE, the Lycian cities, which had cooperated for some time, organised a formal federation. Xanthos, Patara, Pinara, Olympos, Myra and Tlos were among its six largest members.
lycian-league.r: Strabo describes 23 member cities sending delegates to a common assembly, with the largest cities having three votes, middling ones two and the smallest one. A federal official, the Lyciarch, presided, and the league minted common coins. Its system was later cited in the Federalist Papers.
lycian-league.e: The league kept its autonomy as a Roman ally, but after unrest Claudius annexed Lycia in 43 CE, making it a province, later joined with Pamphylia. The league survived as a provincial council.

lordship-of-chios.t: Genoese lordship of the Zaccaria family on Chios, granted by Byzantium to defend the island against Turkish raiders and lost to a Greek rising in 1329.
lordship-of-chios.o: Benedetto I Zaccaria, a Genoese admiral and merchant who already held the rich alum mines of Phocaea from the Byzantines, occupied Chios in 1304 to protect it from Turkish pirates. Emperor Andronikos II, unable to defend the island himself, recognised Zaccaria rule for a fixed term, which was later renewed.
lordship-of-chios.r: The Zaccaria ruled as nominal Byzantine vassals, but in practice as independent lords. They profited from the island's mastic, wine and silk and from alum trade. Martino Zaccaria built a fleet that fought Turkish raiders successfully, took the title King and Despot of Asia Minor from the Latin pretenders, and struck his own coins.
lordship-of-chios.e: Martino's growing independence alarmed the Byzantines. In 1329 the Chiots rose against him with the support of Andronikos III, who landed with a fleet; Martino was captured and Chios returned to Byzantium. The Genoese came back in 1346, creating the Maona of Chios.

lordship-of-galloway.t: A semi-independent Gaelic lordship in south-west Scotland, whose lords acted almost as kings until the line ended in 1234.
lordship-of-galloway.o: Galloway takes its name from the Gall-Gaidheil, the 'foreign Gaels' of mixed Norse and Gaelic descent who settled the region in the 9th and 10th centuries. Around 1110 Fergus of Galloway emerged as its ruler, styled king in some sources, and married an illegitimate daughter of Henry I of England.
lordship-of-galloway.r: The lords of Galloway ruled a land of cattle and sea-power with its own laws, while founding monasteries such as Dundrennan and Soulseat and reviving the bishopric of Whithorn. Fergus's grandson Roland and great-grandson Alan were great Anglo-Scottish nobles; Alan's fleet raided Ireland and the Kingdom of the Isles.
lordship-of-galloway.e: When Alan died in 1234 without a legitimate son, Alexander II divided Galloway between his daughters, crushing a revolt. The lordship became part of the Kingdom of Scotland; Alan's grandson was the future King John Balliol.

laanemaa.t: Coastal county of western Estonia, centred on Lihula, which became the mainland core of the Bishopric of Ösel-Wiek.
laanemaa.o: Läänemaa, known in Latin as Rotalia or Maritima, covered the western coast of Estonia facing the islands of Saaremaa and Hiiumaa. Its main stronghold was at Lihula, and the area had close ties with the islanders across the narrow straits.
laanemaa.r: Its elders led farming and fishing communities on the low coastal land. In 1220 a Swedish crusade under King John I occupied Lihula, but the Oeselians attacked and wiped out the garrison, ending Sweden's first attempt to gain a foothold in Estonia.
laanemaa.e: Läänemaa was subdued by the Germans and Danes by 1224 and became the mainland part of the Bishopric of Ösel-Wiek, whose bishops first resided at Lihula and later at Haapsalu (Hapsal). The name survives in Lääne county.

latvian-socialist-soviet-republic.t: Bolshevik Latvia of 1918-1920, led by Pēteris Stučka, which briefly held Riga before being driven out in the Latvian War of Independence.
latvian-socialist-soviet-republic.o: After Germany's defeat, the Red Army and the Latvian Riflemen invaded Latvia. On 17 December 1918 a Soviet government under Pēteris Stučka proclaimed the Latvian Socialist Soviet Republic, and on 3 January 1919 it took Riga, forcing the national government of Kārlis Ulmanis to retreat to Liepāja.
latvian-socialist-soviet-republic.r: The Soviet government nationalised land, industry and housing and created revolutionary tribunals, which carried out hundreds of executions. Food requisitioning caused famine in Riga. Its army controlled most of Latvia in early 1919, and it adopted a constitution in January.
latvian-socialist-soviet-republic.e: German Freikorps and the Baltic Landeswehr, with Latvian national units, recaptured Riga on 22 May 1919. The Soviet government held on in Latgale until Latvian and Polish forces took Daugavpils in January 1920, and it was dissolved. The Republic of Latvia signed peace with Soviet Russia in August 1920.

lordship-of-ameland.t: A Wadden Sea island that remained a free lordship under the Cammingha family, neutral in the wars around it, until the Orange-Nassau family bought it.
lordship-of-ameland.o: Ameland lay outside the authority of the counts of Holland and the Frisian lands, and from the 15th century the Cammingha family, Frisian chieftains, ruled it as lords, a status the register dates to 1424. They defended its independence against the Habsburgs and later the Dutch provinces.
lordship-of-ameland.r: The island was small, with villages such as Hollum, Ballum and Nes, living from fishing, farming and later whaling, with many 17th-century whaling commanders. Its lords claimed neutrality, which let islanders trade during wars. Ameland accepted the Reformation and governed itself through local courts under the lord.
lordship-of-ameland.e: After the Cammingha line ended, the lordship was bought in 1704 for the Orange-Nassau family. It lost its separate status in the Batavian period and became part of Friesland in the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

lordship-of-andros.t: Latin lordship on the Cycladic island of Andros, a vassal of the Duchy of the Archipelago that survived until the Ottoman takeover in 1566.
lordship-of-andros.o: Around 1207 the Venetian Marino Dandolo, a companion of Marco Sanudo, conquered Andros from the Byzantines and held it as a fief under Sanudo's Duchy of the Archipelago. The island was fertile and well placed on the sea route between Euboea and the central Cyclades.
lordship-of-andros.r: A small Italian elite held the castle and the best land, while Greek Orthodox islanders produced silk, wine and grain. The lordship passed among Venetian families, including the Ghisi, Sanudo and Zeno, and was disputed in dynastic quarrels with the dukes of Naxos. From 1384 the Sommaripa family, starting with Crusino I, ruled it for most of its remaining history.
lordship-of-andros.e: Increasing Turkish raids left Andros dependent on Venetian protection and Ottoman tolerance. In 1566, when the Ottomans removed the last Crispo duke of Naxos, they also ended Sommaripa rule on Andros, which was annexed to the empire.

lordship-of-plauen.t: Vogtland lordship of the imperial advocates of Plauen, whose family gave the Vogtland its name and a Grand Master to the Teutonic Order.
lordship-of-plauen.o: The advocates of Weida, imperial officials whose men were all named Henry, governed lands on the upper Elster and Saale for the Hohenstaufen emperors. From about 1209 a branch ruled Plauen, and the whole region came to be called the Vogtland after their title. Over time they treated the office as a hereditary lordship.
lordship-of-plauen.r: The lords ruled a hilly district of farms, forests and small towns from Plauen. Family members served as knights and administrators, and Heinrich von Plauen defended Marienburg after the Battle of Grunwald and became Grand Master of the State of the Teutonic Order. The Wettins and Bohemian kings steadily eroded their power; in 1466 the Wettins took Plauen.
lordship-of-plauen.e: Henry IV of Plauen, Burgrave of Meissen and Bohemian chancellor, recovered Plauen in 1547. His line died out in 1572 and the lands passed to Saxony. Another branch of the family survived as the princes of Reuss, rulers in eastern Thuringia until 1918.

lordship-of-beaujeu.t: The barony of the Beaujolais hills between Lyon and Mâcon, whose lords founded Villefranche-sur-Saône and served the French crown before it passed to the Bourbons.
lordship-of-beaujeu.o: The lords of Beaujeu appear in the 10th century as castellans in the hills west of the Saône, between the counts of Mâcon and Forez and the archbishops of Lyon. Their castle at Beaujeu gave its name to the Beaujolais, and they gradually brought the surrounding parishes under their control.
lordship-of-beaujeu.r: The lords built a compact barony and around 1140 founded Villefranche-sur-Saône, which became its commercial centre and later capital. Vineyards and the Saône trade underpinned its economy. Lords such as Humbert V, constable of France, rose high in royal service, and the family married into the houses of Forez and Savoy.
lordship-of-beaujeu.e: In 1400 the last lord, Edward II, childless and in debt, left the Beaujolais to Louis II, Duke of Bourbon, and it joined the Duchy of Bourbon. After the Bourbon lands were confiscated in 1527, it passed through several holders before ending up in the Orléans family.

lordship-of-limpurg.t: Franconian-Swabian lordship of the Schenks of Limpurg, hereditary imperial cupbearers, ruled from Gaildorf until the line died out in 1713.
lordship-of-limpurg.o: The Schenks of Limpurg were imperial ministerials who held the hereditary office of cupbearer of the Empire. Around 1230 they built Limpurg castle above Schwäbisch Hall, and they acquired lands in the Kocher valley and the forests of the Limpurg uplands, forming a lordship held directly from the Empire.
lordship-of-limpurg.r: The lordship was rural, with forests, farms and small towns such as Gaildorf and Obersontheim. Relations with the Free Imperial City of Schwäbisch Hall were tense, and in 1541 the Schenks sold Limpurg castle to the city. The family adopted Lutheranism and divided into branches with residences at Gaildorf and Sontheim. The imperial cupbearer title gave them a ceremonial role at coronations.
lordship-of-limpurg.e: The last male Schenk died in 1713, and the lands were divided among female heirs and their families, with Prussia claiming part of the inheritance. The fragmented Limpurg lands were mediatised and passed to Württemberg in 1806.

lordship-of-utrecht.t: The former bishops' lands around Utrecht under Habsburg rule, where the Union of Utrecht, founding act of the Dutch Republic, was signed in 1579.
lordship-of-utrecht.o: Weakened by wars with Guelders and Holland, Bishop Henry of Bavaria transferred the temporal power of the Prince-Bishopric of Utrecht to Charles V in 1528. The Nedersticht became the Lordship of Utrecht, one of the Seventeen Provinces of the Habsburg Netherlands.
lordship-of-utrecht.r: Charles V built the Vredenburg castle in Utrecht to control the city and governed through a stadtholder shared with Holland. The province kept its own estates, with the cathedral chapters forming an influential first estate. The bishop remained a purely spiritual figure, and Utrecht became an archbishopric in 1559.
lordship-of-utrecht.e: Utrecht joined the Revolt; the citizens demolished Vredenburg in 1577, and the Union of Utrecht was concluded there in 1579. After the Act of Abjuration in 1581 it became a province of the Dutch Republic.

larissa.t: Chief city of Thessaly on the Peneios river, seat of the powerful Aleuad family and of the Thessalian League.
larissa.o: Larissa grew on a low hill by the Peneios in the plain of northern Thessaly, inhabited since the Neolithic. In the Archaic period it became the leading city of the Thessalian League under the Aleuad family, who claimed descent from Heracles. Aleuas the Red was credited with organising Thessaly into four districts.
larissa.r: Larissa's landed aristocracy ruled over serfs called penestai and bred horses for cavalry. The Aleuad Thorax supported Xerxes in 480 BCE. Later Larissa welcomed the sophist Gorgias, and Hippocrates died there. The Aleuads invited Philip II of the Kingdom of Macedon to intervene against the tyrants of Pherae.
larissa.e: From the 340s BCE Larissa was effectively under Macedonian control. After Flamininus proclaimed Greek freedom in 196 BCE it became the seat of the revived Thessalian League and passed under Roman control in 146 BCE; it is a major Greek city today.
