lithuanian-byelorussian-ssr.t: Litbel, a short-lived Soviet republic joining Lithuania and Belarus in 1919, created as a buffer against Poland and soon overrun.
lithuanian-byelorussian-ssr.o: In February 1919 Moscow merged the Soviet republics of Lithuania and Byelorussia, including the Socialist Soviet Republic of Byelorussia, into a single Lithuanian-Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic, known as Litbel. Its capital was Vilnius, and Vincas Mickevicius-Kapsukas chaired its council of people's commissars.
lithuanian-byelorussian-ssr.r: Litbel was a Bolshevik state with nationalised land and industry, governed by the Communist Party and backed by the Red Army. It was intended as a buffer between Soviet Russia and Poland, but it had little popular support among Lithuanians, Poles or Belarusians and controlled only part of the territory it claimed.
lithuanian-byelorussian-ssr.e: The Polish army captured Vilnius in April 1919 and Minsk in August, and the Lithuanian army pushed from the west. Litbel effectively ceased to exist by the summer of 1919. The Byelorussian SSR was re-created in 1920.

lower-navarre.t: The fragment of the Kingdom of Navarre north of the Pyrenees, ruled by the Albret kings and the future Henry IV until its union with France in 1620.
lower-navarre.o: Ferdinand of Aragon conquered the Kingdom of Navarre south of the Pyrenees in 1512. The Albret kings kept a small Basque-speaking territory on the northern side around Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port and Saint-Palais, which Charles V gave up around 1530 as too hard to hold.
lower-navarre.r: The Albret monarchs, who also ruled neighbouring Béarn, kept the royal title and Navarre's own estates and courts, with Saint-Palais as the seat of government. Queen Jeanne d'Albret converted to Calvinism and promoted it, though most Basques stayed Catholic. Her son Henry III of Navarre became Henry IV of France in 1589.
lower-navarre.e: Henry IV kept Navarre separate from France. In 1620 Louis XIII issued an edict uniting Lower Navarre and Béarn with the Kingdom of France, and French kings were styled 'King of France and Navarre' until 1830.

lordship-of-lemnos.t: Venetian family lordship on the northern Aegean island of Lemnos after the Fourth Crusade, whose lords bore the title of megadux of the Latin Empire.
lordship-of-lemnos.o: Around 1207 the Venetian noble Filocalo Navigajoso seized Lemnos from the Byzantines as part of the Latin carve-up of the Aegean after the Fourth Crusade. The Latin emperor named him megadux, grand duke, giving him a high rank in the Latin Empire, and his heirs kept both title and island.
lordship-of-lemnos.r: Little is known of how the Navigajoso governed. They held the island as a hereditary fief, collecting revenues from a Greek Orthodox population of farmers and herders, and depended on their link to Venice and the Latin Empire for support. Lemnos was valued for its grain and its position near the Dardanelles.
lordship-of-lemnos.e: After the Byzantines recaptured Constantinople in 1261, the island was exposed. The admiral Licario, serving Michael VIII Palaiologos, besieged the Navigajoso and took Lemnos around 1278, returning it to Byzantine rule.

libu.t: The Libyan people west of Egypt whose attacks on the Delta alarmed the pharaohs and whose name became the Greek word 'Libya'.
libu.o: The Libu (Rebu) lived along the coast of what is now eastern Libya, in Cyrenaica and Marmarica. They appear in Egyptian records from the 13th century BCE, when, together with the Meshwesh and seafaring peoples, they tried to move into the fertile western Delta.
libu.r: Little is known of their internal organisation beyond rule by chiefs. Around 1208 BCE their chief Meryey, son of Did, led a coalition including Sea Peoples against Merneptah, who defeated it at Perire and claimed over six thousand Libyans killed. Ramesses III fought them again. Like the Meshwesh, many were later settled in the western Delta, where chiefs bearing the title 'Great Chief of the Libu' ruled from Sais by the 8th century BCE.
libu.e: The Libu chieftaincy at Sais gave rise to the Twenty-fourth Dynasty of Egypt and later the Twenty-sixth Dynasty. Their name passed to the Greeks as 'Libya', used for all of Africa west of Egypt.

landgraviate-of-hesse-homburg.t: Small Hessian landgraviate in the Taunus, home of the soldier-prince of Kleist's drama and later of a celebrated spa and casino.
landgraviate-of-hesse-homburg.o: Hesse-Homburg was established in 1622 when Landgrave George II of Hesse-Darmstadt granted Homburg vor der Höhe to his brother Frederick I as an appanage. It remained dependent on Hesse-Darmstadt for most of its history rather than a fully sovereign state.
landgraviate-of-hesse-homburg.r: Frederick II, who lost a leg in Swedish service and commanded the Brandenburg cavalry at Fehrbellin in 1675, built the baroque palace and inspired Heinrich von Kleist's play The Prince of Homburg. Later landgraves welcomed Huguenot and Waldensian refugees. In the 19th century Homburg grew into a fashionable spa, and its casino, opened in 1841, drew visitors from across Europe.
landgraviate-of-hesse-homburg.e: Hesse-Homburg was mediatised to Hesse-Darmstadt in 1806 but restored as a sovereign member of the German Confederation in 1815, gaining Meisenheim. The line died out in 1866, the lands passed briefly to the Grand Duchy of Hesse and were then annexed by Prussia.

lordship-of-groningen.t: The city of Groningen and its surrounding Ommelanden under Habsburg rule, a reluctant province that joined the Dutch Republic only after a siege in 1594.
lordship-of-groningen.o: Groningen, a Hanseatic city that dominated the Frisian Ommelanden around it, resisted Saxon rule and placed itself under Charles of Egmond, duke of Guelders, in 1515. When Guelders weakened, the city and countryside accepted Charles V as lord in 1536, joining the Habsburg Netherlands.
lordship-of-groningen.r: Stad en Lande, the city and the lands, was governed by its own estates in which the city and the rural Ommelanden constantly quarrelled over staple rights and taxes. The Habsburgs ruled through a stadtholder. Groningen traded grain and cattle and kept close ties with the German Hanse.
lordship-of-groningen.e: In 1580 the stadtholder Rennenberg went over to the Spanish side, keeping Groningen royalist. Maurice of Nassau besieged and took the city in 1594, and it joined the Dutch Republic as a province.

lordship-of-molina.t: A semi-independent Castilian lordship on the borders of Aragon, ruled by the Lara family and governed by its own celebrated fuero.
lordship-of-molina.o: Alfonso I of Aragon took Molina around 1129. It was soon granted to the Castilian noble Manrique Pérez de Lara, who held it under Castilian overlordship and in 1154 gave the town and its land a fuero, a charter of rights for settlers.
lordship-of-molina.r: Molina was a frontier lordship of herders and settlers between Castile and Aragon, defended by its great castle. Its lords issued laws, minted coins and raised troops with considerable autonomy. In the 13th century the heiress Mafalda married the infante Alfonso de Molina, brother of Ferdinand III, tying it closer to the Castilian royal family.
lordship-of-molina.e: Blanca Alfonso de Molina died childless in 1293, and the lordship passed to her half-sister María de Molina, queen of Sancho IV, and thus to the Crown of Castile. Spanish kings still bear the title Lord of Molina.

lordship-of-montpellier.t: The merchant town of Languedoc whose Guilhem lords founded a dynasty, whose university taught medicine, and where King James I of Aragon was born.
lordship-of-montpellier.o: In 985 the count of Melgueil granted lands at Montpellier to a man named Guilhem, whose descendants, all named William, ruled the growing town as lords. Montpellier rose quickly in the 11th and 12th centuries as a market and staging post on the road from Italy to Spain.
lordship-of-montpellier.r: The lords governed with an active merchant community and a strong consulate. Montpellier traded spices, cloth and dyes across the Mediterranean, and its medical school, recognised as a faculty in 1220, became one of the most famous in Europe. In 1204 the heiress Marie of Montpellier married Peter II of Aragon; their son James I was born there in 1208.
lordship-of-montpellier.e: The lordship passed to the Aragonese crown and then to the Kingdom of Majorca. In 1349 the hard-pressed James III of Majorca sold Montpellier to Philip VI, and it joined the Kingdom of France.

lithuanian-soviet-socialist-republic.t: Soviet Lithuania, created by the annexation of 1940, which became the first Soviet republic to declare independence in 1990.
lithuanian-soviet-socialist-republic.o: Under the secret protocols of the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, the Soviet Union occupied the Republic of Lithuania in June 1940. A rigged election produced a People's Seimas that requested admission to the Soviet Union, and Lithuania was annexed in August 1940, with Vilnius, regained in 1939, as its capital.
lithuanian-soviet-socialist-republic.r: Soviet rule brought nationalisation, collectivisation and mass deportations in 1941 and after the war. German occupation in 1941-1944 saw the murder of most of Lithuania's Jews. After 1944 armed partisans, the Forest Brothers, resisted until the early 1950s. Antanas Sniečkus led the Communist Party from 1940 to 1974, and the republic industrialised while Catholic dissent remained strong.
lithuanian-soviet-socialist-republic.e: In 1988 the Sąjūdis reform movement emerged, and in 1989 the Lithuanian Communist Party under Algirdas Brazauskas broke from Moscow. On 11 March 1990 the Supreme Council declared the restoration of the independent Republic of Lithuania, recognised internationally in 1991.

lordship-of-sidon.t: One of the four great baronies of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, whose lords built Sidon's Sea Castle and the fortress of Beaufort.
lordship-of-sidon.o: Sidon surrendered in December 1110 to Baldwin I, helped by the Norwegian king Sigurd the Crusader and his fleet. The city was granted to Eustace Grenier, and his descendants held it as one of the kingdom's chief lordships.
lordship-of-sidon.r: The lordship included the coast between Beirut and Tyre and inland castles such as Beaufort above the Litani. Reynald of Sidon spoke Arabic and was respected by Saladin, with whom he negotiated while holding Beaufort in 1189-1190. The Sea Castle on an island in the harbour was built in 1228. Sugar and trade with Damascus supported the economy.
lordship-of-sidon.e: Lost in 1187 and recovered in the 13th century, Sidon was sacked by the Mongols in 1260, and Julian Grenier sold it to the Templars, who held it until the Mamluks took it in 1291.

lordship-of-rhodes.t: Independent Byzantine lordship on Rhodes under the Gabalas family after the fall of Constantinople in 1204, later absorbed by the Empire of Nicaea.
lordship-of-rhodes.o: When the Fourth Crusade broke up the Byzantine Empire in 1204, the Greek official Leo Gabalas took control of Rhodes and neighbouring islands and ruled them as his own domain, styling himself Caesar and lord of Rhodes and the Cyclades.
lordship-of-rhodes.r: Gabalas ruled as an independent Greek lord with a fleet that let him trade and bargain. Under pressure from John III Vatatzes of Nicaea, who sent an expedition in 1233, he accepted Nicaean overlordship. In 1234 he made a treaty with Venice granting its merchants trading rights while securing Venetian support. His brother John Gabalas succeeded him around 1240.
lordship-of-rhodes.e: In 1248 the Genoese seized Rhodes in a surprise attack. Nicaea recaptured the island around 1250 and ruled it directly as part of the Empire of Nicaea. In 1310 it fell to the Knights Hospitaller, becoming Hospitaller Rhodes.

lordship-of-oultrejordain.t: The Crusader lordship east of the Jordan, whose castles of Kerak and Montreal controlled the routes between Syria, Egypt and Arabia.
lordship-of-oultrejordain.o: Baldwin I built the castle of Montreal at Shobak in 1115 to control the land beyond the Jordan, and the region was organised as a lordship from around 1118. Payen the Butler built the great castle of Kerak in 1142, which became its centre.
lordship-of-oultrejordain.r: The lordship taxed the caravans and pilgrims moving between Damascus, Egypt and the Hijaz, and the Bedouin of the region. It passed to Philip of Milly and then, through the heiress Stephanie of Milly, to Raynald of Chatillon in 1176. Raynald raided the Red Sea coast in 1182-1183, threatening Mecca and Medina, and attacked a caravan in breach of a truce, provoking Saladin.
lordship-of-oultrejordain.e: Raynald was executed by Saladin after the battle of Hattin in 1187. Kerak surrendered after a long siege in 1188 and Montreal in 1189; the castles became Ayyubid strongholds.

lebedos.t: Small Ionian city between Teos and Colophon, one of the twelve of the Ionian League, later home of the travelling Dionysiac actors.
lebedos.o: Lebedos was settled by Ionian Greeks, traditionally under Andraemon, son of Codrus, on the coast between Teos and Colophon c. 1000 BCE. Though small, it was one of the twelve members of the Ionian League.
lebedos.r: Little is known of its government. It lived from farming and fishing and had hot springs nearby. Lebedos fell to Lydia and then to the Achaemenid Empire, and paid tribute to Athens as a member of the Delian League. It revolted from Athens in 412 BCE.
lebedos.e: Lysimachus moved many of its inhabitants to Ephesus c. 290 BCE. The Ptolemies refounded it as Ptolemais, and the guild of Dionysiac artists later settled there. Lebedos passed into Roman Asia after 133 BCE; Horace described it as nearly deserted.

lordships-of-schonburg.t: Cluster of lordships in western Saxony held by the Schönburg family for six centuries, balanced uneasily between imperial immediacy and Saxon control.
lordships-of-schonburg.o: The Schönburgs were imperial ministerials from the Saale region near Naumburg. From about 1170 they were granted lands in the Pleissenland, the imperial territory around Altenburg, and built up lordships along the Zwickauer Mulde centred on Glauchau, later adding Waldenburg, Lichtenstein and Hartenstein. These were held directly from the Empire, which gave the family the standing of minor imperial lords.
lordships-of-schonburg.r: The lordships were ruled by several branches of the family from castles in Glauchau and Waldenburg, with small towns, farmland and later textile crafts in the valley. The family adopted Lutheranism in the 16th century. Their position was squeezed by the neighbouring Wettin rulers of Saxony, who held some Schönburg lands as fiefs and steadily claimed sovereignty over the rest.
lordships-of-schonburg.e: By the recesses agreed with the Electorate of Saxony, culminating in 1740, the Schönburgs accepted Saxon sovereignty while keeping special rights of administration and justice. These lingered into the 19th century, and the family remained major landowners in Saxony until 1945.

lordship-of-werle.t: Mecklenburg lordship of the Niklotid princes centred on Güstrow, who styled themselves princes of the Wends until the line died out in 1436.
lordship-of-werle.o: In the division of Mecklenburg among the sons of Henry Borwin II in 1229, Nicholas I received the eastern lands around Güstrow and the castle of Werle. His line ruled as lords of Werle, alongside their cousins in Mecklenburg, Rostock and Parchim-Richenberg, all descended from the Obotrite prince Niklot.
lordship-of-werle.r: The lords ruled a land of lakes, farmland and small towns such as Güstrow, Waren and Malchow, which grew with German settlement. They repeatedly split the territory among branches such as Werle-Güstrow and Werle-Goldberg. From the 15th century they used the title Prince of the Wends, recalling their Slavic ancestry, while their power slowly waned beside the Mecklenburg dukes.
lordship-of-werle.e: The last lord, William of Werle, died in 1436 without a son, and his lands passed to the Duchy of Mecklenburg. The dukes adopted the title Prince of the Wends, and Güstrow later became a ducal residence.

lugi.t: People of eastern Sutherland recorded by Ptolemy, whose name may honour the Celtic god Lugus.
lugi.o: The Lugi are known only from Ptolemy's Geography of about 150, which places them in the far north of Scotland, usually located on the east coast of Sutherland around the Dornoch Firth and the Brora area, between the Decantae and the Cornavii (Caithness). Their name may derive from the god Lugus or from a word for raven.
lugi.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers or customs. Eastern Sutherland has many brochs along its river valleys and coast, such as those of Strath Brora, suggesting communities led by local families who controlled grazing and farmland.
lugi.e: The Lugi vanish from the record after Ptolemy. Their territory later formed part of the lands of the northern Picts and then of the Norse earldom of Orkney before being drawn into the Scottish kingdom.

lilybaeum.t: Carthaginian fortress city at Sicily's western tip, founded after the fall of Motya, which withstood Pyrrhus and a nine-year Roman siege.
lilybaeum.o: After Dionysius I destroyed Motya in 397 BCE, Carthage settled the survivors on Cape Lilybaeum, the westernmost point of Sicily. The new city, on a headland with a sheltered harbour facing Africa, became Carthage's main base on the island.
lilybaeum.r: Lilybaeum was a heavily fortified port with walls, towers and a deep ditch. Its population was mainly Punic with Greek elements, and its trade linked Carthage with Sicily. It successfully resisted Pyrrhus in 276 BCE and, in the First Punic War, a Roman siege by land and sea from 250 to 241 BCE.
lilybaeum.e: Carthage ceded Lilybaeum to Rome by the treaty ending the First Punic War in 241 BCE. It became the seat of one of the quaestors of Roman Sicily, a post Cicero held in 75 BCE. It later became the Arab port of Marsa Allah, modern Marsala.

latvian-soviet-socialist-republic.t: Soviet Latvia, annexed in 1940 and restored to independence in 1990-1991 after the mass movements of the Baltic Way era.
latvian-soviet-socialist-republic.o: After a Soviet ultimatum in June 1940, the Red Army occupied the Republic of Latvia. A rigged election produced a parliament that requested admission to the Soviet Union, and Latvia was annexed in August 1940. German occupation followed in 1941-1944, before Soviet rule returned.
latvian-soviet-socialist-republic.r: Soviet power brought nationalisation, collectivisation and mass deportations in June 1941 and March 1949. Riga became a major industrial centre, producing radios, railway carriages and the RAF minibuses, which drew large numbers of Russian-speaking workers, so that Latvians fell to barely half the population. Communist leaders included Arvīds Pelše and Augusts Voss, and a 1959 purge removed national communists.
latvian-soviet-socialist-republic.e: The Popular Front of Latvia mobilised mass support, including the Baltic Way human chain of 1989. On 4 May 1990 the Supreme Council under Anatolijs Gorbunovs declared the restoration of independence, completed on 21 August 1991, restoring the Republic of Latvia.

lachish.t: Lachish, a major Canaanite city of the Shephelah lowlands and Egyptian vassal in the Amarna age, later the second city of Judah.
lachish.o: Lachish, at Tel Lachish west of Hebron, became a large fortified city in the Middle Bronze Age, protected by a steep glacis. It controlled the fertile Shephelah between the coastal plain and the Judaean hills and the roads leading to Egypt.
lachish.r: In the Late Bronze Age its kings, including Zimreddi and Shipti-Ba'lu, were vassals of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom and wrote to the pharaoh in the Amarna letters. Excavations revealed a temple in the old moat, the Fosse Temple, and inscriptions in early alphabetic script.
lachish.e: The Canaanite city was destroyed and abandoned in the 12th century BCE, probably during the collapse of Egyptian rule. Rebuilt in the Iron Age, it became a fortress of the Kingdom of Judah, famously besieged by Sennacherib of the Assyrian Empire in 701 BCE.

cr.a: Cartographers and surveyors of the British East India Company

lycian-dynasts.t: The Lycian dynasts, local rulers of Xanthos and other cities who governed Lycia under Persian overlordship and built striking tombs.
lycian-dynasts.o: In c. 540 BCE the Persian general Harpagus conquered Lycia; Herodotus tells that the men of Xanthos killed their families and died fighting. Afterwards a dynasty at Xanthos, perhaps descended from Harpagus, and rival dynasts in other cities ruled Lycia as vassals of the Achaemenid Empire.
lycian-dynasts.r: The dynasts minted silver coins with Lycian legends and raised pillar tombs and temple-tombs, such as the Nereid Monument of Erbbina, now in the British Museum. The Inscribed Pillar at Xanthos carries the longest known Lycian text. Lycian culture blended Anatolian traditions with Greek art.
lycian-dynasts.e: In the 4th century BCE Pericles of Limyra briefly united Lycia and joined the revolt against Persia, but Mausolus of Hecatomnid Caria took control c. 360 BCE. The dynasts disappeared, and Lycia later reorganised as the Lycian League.

lordship-of-arsuf.t: A coastal lordship of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, near which Richard the Lionheart defeated Saladin in 1191.
lordship-of-arsuf.o: Arsuf, the ancient Apollonia, surrendered to Baldwin I in 1101 with the help of a Genoese fleet. It became a lordship within the royal domain and was later granted to vassal families.
lordship-of-arsuf.r: The lordship was small, based on a fortified town and harbour on the cliffs north of Jaffa. On 7 September 1191 Richard I won the battle of Arsuf nearby, securing the coast for the Third Crusade. In the 13th century it was held by a branch of the Ibelin family, including John of Ibelin, lord of Arsuf and regent of the kingdom. Debts led Balian of Arsuf to lease it to the Hospitallers in 1261.
lordship-of-arsuf.e: Baybars besieged Arsuf in 1265; after forty days the Hospitaller garrison surrendered and the town was destroyed. Its ruins and castle remain at Apollonia National Park.
ru: John of Ibelin, Lord of Arsuf

lordship-of-phocaea.t: A Genoese lordship on the Aegean coast of Anatolia built on the alum mines that supplied Europe's textile industry.
lordship-of-phocaea.o: In 1275 the Byzantine emperor Michael VIII granted Phocaea and its alum mines to the Genoese brothers Manuel and Benedetto Zaccaria. Alum, essential for fixing dyes in cloth, made the grant extremely valuable.
lordship-of-phocaea.r: The Zaccaria built New Phocaea to protect the mines and dominated the European alum trade, shipping it to Flanders and Italy; Benedetto also took Chios in 1304. The colony employed local Greek labour and paid tribute to Turkish neighbours. The Byzantines retook Phocaea in 1340, but Genoese families, from the 1350s within the circle of the Maona of Chios and the Gattilusio, regained control and held it as Byzantine vassals.
lordship-of-phocaea.e: After the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople, Mehmed II took Old and New Phocaea in 1455, ending Genoese control of the alum trade until new mines were found at Tolfa in Italy.

lordship-of-valencia.t: The Valencian principality of Rodrigo Díaz, El Cid, who conquered the city in 1094 and held it against the Almoravids until his death.
lordship-of-valencia.o: Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, a Castilian noble exiled by Alfonso VI, had built a mercenary career serving the Taifa of Zaragoza and collecting tribute in the east. When the qadi Ibn Jahhaf killed al-Qadir in 1092, Rodrigo besieged Valencia, which surrendered in June 1094.
lordship-of-valencia.r: El Cid ruled as an independent lord, nominally loyal to Alfonso VI. He defeated Almoravid relief armies at Cuarte in 1094 and Bairén in 1097, burnt Ibn Jahhaf alive and turned the great mosque into a cathedral under Bishop Jerome of Périgord. Most of the Muslim population remained, paying taxes to his garrison.
lordship-of-valencia.e: El Cid died in 1099. His widow Jimena held Valencia until 1102, when Alfonso VI judged it indefensible, evacuated the Christians and burnt the city. The Almoravids entered in May 1102. The story inspired the epic Cantar de mio Cid.

lordship-of-nikola-altomanovic.t: Short-lived lordship of the Serbian magnate Nikola Altomanović, the largest in western Serbia after the collapse of Dušan's empire.
lordship-of-nikola-altomanovic.o: Nikola Altomanović, son of a nobleman in Stefan Dušan's service, built up lands in the 1360s as Uroš V's authority faded. By about 1371 he held a broad territory from Rudnik and Užice to the borders of Ragusa and Hum.
lordship-of-nikola-altomanovic.r: Nikola ruled from Užice as an independent lord, taxing the silver mines of Rudnik and quarrelling with Ragusa over trade dues. He was aggressive towards his neighbours, plotting against Prince Lazar and Tvrtko I of the Banate of Bosnia.
lordship-of-nikola-altomanovic.e: In 1373 Lazar and Tvrtko, backed by Louis I of Hungary, defeated him; he was captured at Užice and blinded. His lands were divided between Lazar's Moravian Serbia, Bosnia and Đurađ I Balšić of Zeta.

lesser-armenia.t: Lesser Armenia, a highland kingdom on the upper Euphrates that passed between Pontus, Galatian chiefs and Roman client kings.
lesser-armenia.o: After Alexander's conquest, the mountainous land west of the upper Euphrates was ruled by local Armenian dynasts, separate from the Kingdom of Armenia (Orontid). In the late 2nd century BCE its ruler Antipater ceded it to Mithridates VI of the Kingdom of Pontus, who built many fortresses to store his treasures.
lesser-armenia.r: Lesser Armenia was a land of pastures and fortified hilltops. After Pompey defeated Mithridates in 66 BCE, he founded Nicopolis on the battlefield and gave the region to the Galatian king Deiotarus. Rome later used it as a reward for loyal client kings.
lesser-armenia.e: Its last king, Aristobulus, a great-grandson of Herod, ruled until c. 71 CE. Vespasian annexed Lesser Armenia to the Roman province of Cappadocia in 72 CE.

lordship-of-rimini.t: The Malatesta lordship of Rimini, home of Sigismondo Malatesta's Tempio Malatestiano and of the tragedy of Paolo and Francesca.
lordship-of-rimini.o: Malatesta da Verucchio, leader of the Guelphs of Rimini, drove out the Ghibelline Parcitadi family in 1295 and made himself lord of the city. His heirs ruled Rimini as papal vicars and spread through Romagna and the Marche.
lordship-of-rimini.r: The Malatesta were warlords and condottieri who governed Rimini, Cesena, Fano and other towns. Malatesta's son Gianciotto killed his wife Francesca da Polenta and his brother Paolo, a story Dante told in the Inferno. Sigismondo Pandolfo Malatesta, a brilliant and ruthless captain, had Leon Battista Alberti remodel the church of San Francesco as the Tempio Malatestiano. Pope Pius II publicly condemned Sigismondo in 1462 and took most of his lands.
lordship-of-rimini.e: In 1500 Cesare Borgia drove out Pandolfo IV Malatesta. Venice held Rimini from 1503 to 1509, after which it passed to direct papal rule in the Papal States.

liang-li-gui.t: A brief kingdom in the Hexi Corridor, centred on Wuwei, set up as Sui collapsed and overthrown in 619 by a Sogdian family who handed it to the Tang.
liang-li-gui.o: Li Gui, a wealthy and respected notable of Wuwei (Liangzhou), was chosen by local leaders in 617 to resist the Qin of Xue Ju. He proclaimed himself Prince of Great Liang and in 618 took the title of emperor, controlling the Hexi Corridor oasis cities.
liang-li-gui.r: The state sat astride the Silk Road, and Sogdian merchant families were powerful in its capital. Li Gui at first exchanged friendly letters with Li Yuan, founder of the Tang Dynasty, but refused to accept a subordinate title, insisting on equal imperial status.
liang-li-gui.e: In 619 the Tang envoy An Xinggui, whose Sogdian family was influential in Wuwei, worked with his brother An Xiuren to raise troops against Li Gui. They captured him and delivered him to Chang'an, where he was executed, and the Hexi Corridor passed to Tang rule.

lordship-of-ainos.t: Branch lordship of the Genoese Gattilusi family at the mouth of the Maritsa, controlling trade from Thrace until Mehmed II took it in 1456.
lordship-of-ainos.o: Ainos (Enez), an old Greek port at the mouth of the Hebrus (Maritsa), came under the control of Niccolo Gattilusio, brother of Francesco I Gattilusio of the Lordship of Lesbos, around 1384. It became a separate branch of the family's possessions in the northern Aegean.
lordship-of-ainos.r: The lords of Ainos profited from salt pans, fisheries and river trade with the Thracian interior, and their realm included Samothrace and at times Imbros. They acted as Byzantine vassals and later as Ottoman tributaries. Palamede Gattilusio ruled for about forty years, and the family's inscriptions and fortifications survive on Samothrace and at Enez.
lordship-of-ainos.e: After the death of Palamede in 1455 a succession dispute among his heirs gave Mehmed II an excuse to intervene. In 1456 the Ottomans took Ainos and the lordship ended.

later-zhou.t: The last of the Five Dynasties, whose able emperor Chai Rong began the reunification of China completed by the Song.
later-zhou.o: Guo Wei, a leading general of the Later Han, was forced into rebellion when Emperor Liu Chengyou plotted to kill him in 950. After the emperor's death he took the throne at Kaifeng in 951 as founder of the Zhou dynasty, the first non-Shatuo ruler of the north for decades.
later-zhou.r: Guo Wei lightened taxes and punishments. His adopted son Chai Rong (Emperor Shizong), who succeeded in 954, defeated the Northern Han and Khitan at Gaoping, reorganised the palace army, closed thousands of Buddhist monasteries and melted bronze images for coin. He took the lands between the Huai and Yangtze from Southern Tang in 958 and recovered two of the Sixteen Prefectures from the Liao dynasty in 959.
later-zhou.e: Chai Rong died in 959, leaving a child emperor. In 960 the palace army commander Zhao Kuangyin was proclaimed emperor by his troops at Chenqiao and founded the Song Dynasty, which built on Later Zhou's army and policies.

lusitania.t: The Roman province of western Iberia, roughly modern Portugal and Extremadura, governed from the splendid veteran colony of Emerita Augusta.
lusitania.o: Lusitania was carved out of Hispania Ulterior by Augustus after the Cantabrian Wars, with the division under way from 27 BCE. Its capital, Emerita Augusta (Mérida), was founded in 25 BCE for veterans of those wars. It covered the lands of the Lusitanians, Vettones and Celtici between the Douro and the Guadiana.
lusitania.r: An imperial legate governed the province, among them the future emperor Otho from 58 to 68 CE. Emerita grew into one of the great cities of the West, with its theatre, amphitheatre and long bridge over the Guadiana. Olisipo (Lisbon) and Pax Iulia (Beja) were other centres, and the economy rested on farming, mining and fish sauce. Christianity spread early; Eulalia of Mérida was martyred in 304.
lusitania.e: In 409 Vandals, Alans and Suebi crossed into Hispania, and the Alans settled in Lusitania. In 439 the Suebic king Rechila took Emerita, ending effective Roman rule. The province's name later became a poetic name for Portugal.

leptis-magna.t: A Phoenician trading port on the Libyan coast that grew rich under Carthage and later became one of Rome's great African cities.
leptis-magna.o: Leptis (Lpqy in Punic) was founded by Phoenician settlers at the mouth of the Wadi Lebda, east of modern Tripoli, probably in the 7th century BCE. With Oea and Sabratha it formed the three Emporia that later gave Tripolitania its name, linking Mediterranean shipping with caravan routes across the Sahara.
leptis-magna.r: The city was governed by Punic magistrates (suffetes) and a council, and Carthaginian Punic remained its official language long into Roman times. As part of the Punic Empire it was so wealthy that Livy says it paid Carthage a talent a day in tribute. Its farmland produced olive oil and grain, and its merchants handled gold, ivory and slaves from the desert trade.
leptis-magna.e: Masinissa of Numidia seized the Emporia in the 160s BCE, and Leptis later allied with Rome against Jugurtha. Having backed Juba I in Caesar's civil war, it was fined three million pounds of olive oil a year in 46 BCE and absorbed into Roman Africa. It later flourished as the birthplace of Septimius Severus.

lacetani.t: An Iberian people of inland Catalonia who resisted Rome during the Second Punic War and Cato's campaign of 195 BCE.
lacetani.o: The Lacetani lived in the interior of Catalonia, roughly in the modern comarques of Bages, Anoia and Solsonès, from about the 5th century BCE. They were part of the Iberian culture of the north-east and neighbours of the Ilergetes and Ausetani.
lacetani.r: Their society of fortified hilltop villages lived from farming and herding. Ancient writers, mainly Livy, record them only in wartime, and their name is easily confused with the coastal Laietani, so many details are uncertain.
lacetani.e: They fought the Romans under Gnaeus Scipio in 218 BCE and again in the north-eastern revolt of 197 to 195 BCE, when Cato stormed their chief town. Afterwards they were absorbed into Hispania Citerior and their name faded.

lordship-of-brecknock.t: A marcher lordship in the Usk valley created by Bernard de Neufmarche's conquest of the Welsh kingdom of Brycheiniog.
lordship-of-brecknock.o: Bernard de Neufmarche invaded the kingdom of Brycheiniog in the late 11th century and killed Rhys ap Tewdwr of the Kingdom of Deheubarth near Brecon in 1093. He built Brecon Castle and founded Brecon Priory, granting lands to his followers.
lordship-of-brecknock.r: Brecknock was governed as a marcher lordship with its own courts and military obligations, a Norman lowland lordship over a largely Welsh upland population. It passed by marriage to the de Braose family and then to the de Bohuns, earls of Hereford, and later to the Staffords, dukes of Buckingham.
lordship-of-brecknock.e: Edward Stafford, Duke of Buckingham, was executed in 1521 and the lordship came to the crown. The Laws in Wales Act of 1536 made Brecknock a shire, which survives as part of Powys.

lordship-of-mechelen.t: A small separate lordship between Brabant and Antwerp that became the judicial and court capital of the Burgundian and Habsburg Netherlands.
lordship-of-mechelen.o: Mechelen was long divided between the prince-bishops of Liège and the Berthout family, under constant pressure from Brabant. In 1333 the bishop sold his rights to Louis of Nevers, count of Flanders, and after disputes with Brabant the town became a distinct lordship, one of the seventeen provinces of the Low Countries.
lordship-of-mechelen.r: Mechelen was a prosperous cloth town with a tall cathedral tower of St Rumbold. Under the Burgundian State it became seat of the Parliament of Mechelen in 1473, later the Great Council, the supreme court of the Netherlands. Margaret of York and then Margaret of Austria, regent for Charles V, kept their courts there, making it a Renaissance centre.
lordship-of-mechelen.e: In 1559 Mechelen became the seat of the new archbishop, primate of the Netherlands. It stayed with the Spanish Netherlands and the Austrian Netherlands until French annexation in 1795, and is today a city of Belgium.

lusatian-league.t: An alliance of six Upper Lusatian towns, formed in 1346, that dominated the politics and trade of their province for centuries.
lusatian-league.o: In 1346 Bautzen, Görlitz, Zittau, Kamenz, Löbau and Lauban, towns of the Margraviate of Upper Lusatia, then a land of the Kingdom of Bohemia, formed a league to suppress robber knights and protect their trade. Charles IV, as king of Bohemia, approved the alliance, which became a permanent political force.
lusatian-league.r: The six towns met in regular diets, kept a common treasury and troops, and formed a separate estate in the Upper Lusatian diet alongside the nobility. Their wealth came from cloth and linen weaving and from the Via Regia trade road through Görlitz. They fought the Hussites in the 15th century and mostly turned Lutheran in the 16th.
lusatian-league.e: In 1547 Ferdinand I punished the towns for refusing aid in the Schmalkaldic War, confiscating lands and privileges. Upper Lusatia passed to the Electorate of Saxony in 1635, and the league lingered until 1815, when Görlitz and Lauban went to Prussia.

lordship-of-gower.t: A marcher lordship on the Gower peninsula and around Swansea, created by Henry de Beaumont, Earl of Warwick, in the early 12th century.
lordship-of-gower.o: Henry de Beaumont, Earl of Warwick, took Gower from its Welsh rulers around 1106 and built a castle at Swansea. English and Flemish settlers occupied the southern part of the peninsula, which developed a lasting English-speaking character.
lordship-of-gower.r: Gower was divided between an Anglicised lowland 'Englishry' and a Welsh upland 'Welshry'. The lords held their own courts and granted Swansea its first charter. The lordship passed to the de Braose family and later to the Mowbrays and the Herberts, and was repeatedly fought over by the lords of Glamorgan and Welsh princes.
lordship-of-gower.e: The Laws in Wales Act of 1536 attached Gower to the new county of Glamorgan. Its distinct dialect and Anglo-Norman churches remain, and in 1956 it became Britain's first Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty.

lordship-of-ravenstein.t: A small lordship on the Maas that stayed outside the Dutch Republic and became a refuge for Catholics in a Protestant land.
lordship-of-ravenstein.o: Ravenstein grew around a castle on the Maas in north-eastern Brabant. In the 14th century it passed to the house of Cleves, and from 1360 it was held as a separate lordship by Cleves princes, independent of both Brabant and Guelders.
lordship-of-ravenstein.r: The Cleves lords of Ravenstein, notably Adolf of Cleves and his son Philip, were prominent at the Burgundian court. Later the lordship passed to the dukes of Jülich-Berg and the Palatinate-Neuburg family. When the surrounding lands came under the Dutch Republic, Ravenstein remained a Catholic enclave, where priests and believers from the Generality lands could worship freely.
lordship-of-ravenstein.e: The lordship was absorbed into the Batavian Republic around 1800, ending its separate status. It later became part of the province of North Brabant in the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

lordship-of-clandeboye.t: A Gaelic lordship in Antrim and Down held by the Clann Aodha Buidhe O'Neills, who took over the lands of the collapsed Earldom of Ulster.
lordship-of-clandeboye.o: The Clann Aodha Buidhe, descendants of Aodh Buidhe O'Neill, a 13th century king of Tir Eoghain, moved east across the Bann after the collapse of the Earldom of Ulster in 1333. By around 1350 they ruled much of south Antrim and north Down, later divided into Upper and Lower Clandeboye.
lordship-of-clandeboye.r: The lordship's seat was the castle at Castlereagh near Belfast, and its chiefs ruled through Gaelic law, cattle wealth and Scottish gallowglasses. Their territory was later contested by the MacDonnells and by English colonisation attempts, including the Earl of Essex's massacre of Sir Brian MacPhelim O'Neill and his family in 1574.
lordship-of-clandeboye.e: Con O'Neill, the last lord, lost most of his lands to the Scots Hugh Montgomery and James Hamilton in 1605, opening north Down to large-scale Scottish settlement.

lordship-of-haifa.t: A small coastal lordship of the Kingdom of Jerusalem at the foot of Mount Carmel.
lordship-of-haifa.o: Haifa was taken in August 1100 by Tancred with the help of a Venetian fleet, after a stubborn defence in which its Jewish and Muslim inhabitants fought together. It was then granted as a fief, its first known lord being Geldemar Carpenel.
lordship-of-haifa.r: Haifa was a modest lordship with a harbour and the farmland of the Carmel coast, and was at times attached to the Principality of Galilee. It was best known for nearby Mount Carmel, where hermits gathered in the 12th century and the Carmelite order took shape in the early 13th century. Little is recorded about its administration.
lordship-of-haifa.e: Saladin captured Haifa in 1187; it was regained after the Third Crusade and refortified by Louis IX of France in 1250-1252. In 1265 the Mamluk sultan Baybars took and destroyed it.

lordship-of-piedmont.t: The Savoy-Achaea principality in Piedmont, a cadet branch of the house of Savoy that also claimed the Frankish Principality of Achaea in Greece.
lordship-of-piedmont.o: In 1294 Count Amadeus V of the County of Savoy settled his nephew Philip with the family's lands in Piedmont as a dependent appanage. In 1301 Philip married Isabella of Villehardouin, heiress of the Principality of Achaea, and his line kept the title princes of Achaea even after losing Greece.
lordship-of-piedmont.r: Philip and his heirs ruled from Pinerolo over Turin and the towns of the upper Po plain, as vassals of the counts of Savoy. They fought the March of Montferrat and the Marquisate of Saluzzo for control of Piedmont and held assemblies of nobles and towns. Prince Louis founded the University of Turin in 1404.
lordship-of-piedmont.e: Louis died without a legitimate heir in 1418, and his lands returned to his cousin Amadeus VIII of the Duchy of Savoy, uniting Piedmont with Savoy. The heir to the Savoy throne was later styled Prince of Piedmont.

lordship-of-carpi.t: The Pio family's small Emilian lordship, whose humanist prince Alberto III Pio made Carpi a Renaissance showpiece.
lordship-of-carpi.o: In 1319 the Pio family, local nobles, took control of Carpi, a town between Modena and Mantua, with the support of the Bonacolsi. They ruled it as imperial vicars, with the Este and Gonzaga as powerful neighbours.
lordship-of-carpi.r: The Pio governed a small farming territory and its walled town. Alberto III Pio, pupil and patron of the printer Aldus Manutius, rebuilt Carpi around a huge new square with the castle, a new cathedral and porticoes. A diplomat at Rome, he sided with France in the Italian Wars and quarrelled with Erasmus. The family often divided the lordship among relatives.
lordship-of-carpi.e: Alberto's support for France cost him his state: Charles V's forces occupied Carpi, and in 1527 the emperor gave it to Alfonso I d'Este. Carpi then became part of the Este lands of the Duchy of Modena and Reggio.

later-han.t: The shortest of the Five Dynasties, set up at Kaifeng by the Shatuo general Liu Zhiyuan after the Khitan withdrew from northern China in 947.
later-han.o: When the Khitan army of the Liao dynasty took Kaifeng and ended the Later Jin (936-947) at the start of 947, Liu Zhiyuan, Shatuo governor of Hedong at Taiyuan, proclaimed himself emperor. As the Khitan withdrew north under popular resistance, he entered Kaifeng and took over the old court.
later-han.r: Later Han relied on the palace army and on ruthless ministers, and its tax collectors and courts were notorious for harshness. Liu Zhiyuan died in 948, leaving his young son Liu Chengyou under a group of senior ministers and generals.
later-han.e: In 950 Liu Chengyou had leading ministers killed and plotted against the general Guo Wei, who marched on Kaifeng. The emperor was killed in the fighting, and early in 951 Guo Wei founded the Later Zhou. Liu Zhiyuan's brother Liu Chong held Taiyuan as the Northern Han.

landgraviate-of-hesse-marburg.t: A Hessian landgraviate centred on the university town of Marburg, whose division in 1604 set off decades of conflict between Kassel and Darmstadt.
landgraviate-of-hesse-marburg.o: The 1567 division of the Landgraviate of Hesse gave Louis IV, second son of Philip the Magnanimous, about a quarter of the land, centred on Marburg and its university, founded by his father in 1527 as the first Protestant university.
landgraviate-of-hesse-marburg.r: Louis IV was a strict Lutheran who defended orthodoxy against the Calvinist leanings of his brother in Kassel. His land was largely agrarian, with Marburg's castle and university at its centre. He married twice but had no children, and his will required that his heirs keep the Lutheran faith.
landgraviate-of-hesse-marburg.e: When Louis IV died in 1604, his lands were divided between Hesse-Kassel and Hesse-Darmstadt. Maurice of Hesse-Kassel's introduction of Calvinism in Marburg broke the will's terms and started a long dispute that culminated in the Hessian War of 1645 to 1648.

latvian-self-administration.t: Latvian auxiliary administration under German occupation from 1942 to 1945, headed by General Oskars Dankers.
latvian-self-administration.o: Germany placed occupied Latvia in the Generalkommissariat Lettland of Reichskommissariat Ostland. Latvian directors-general were appointed in 1941 to handle local affairs, and in March 1942 the structure was formalised as the Latvian Self-Administration under General Oskars Dankers.
latvian-self-administration.r: The Self-Administration had no political independence and executed German orders on economic, educational and social matters. In 1943 the Germans used it to conscript Latvian men into the Latvian Legion of the Waffen-SS. Most of Latvia's Jews had already been murdered in 1941, notably at Rumbula.
latvian-self-administration.e: The Red Army retook Riga in October 1944, and the administration moved to Courland and then Germany, ending with the German surrender in May 1945. Latvia was again governed as the Latvian Soviet Socialist Republic.

league-of-corinth.t: Alliance of Greek states under Macedonian leadership created by Philip II after Chaeronea, the framework for Alexander the Great's invasion of Persia.
league-of-corinth.o: After defeating Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea in 338 BCE, Philip II called the Greek states to Corinth in 338-337 BCE. They swore to a common peace, forbidding wars and revolutions among members, and named Philip hegemon of a war of revenge against Persia. Sparta alone refused to join.
league-of-corinth.r: A council (synedrion) of delegates, with votes roughly proportional to each member's military strength, met at Corinth and other festival sites and could judge disputes. Members kept their own governments, but Macedonian garrisons held Corinth, Thebes, Chalcis and Ambracia. Alexander had his leadership confirmed in 336 BCE and punished Thebes' revolt in 335 BCE in the league's name.
league-of-corinth.e: The alliance gave Alexander a Greek mandate for his Asian campaign. On news of his death in 323 BCE, Athens and the Aetolians led the Lamian War; Antipater's victory at Crannon in 322 BCE ended both the war and the league. Antigonus and Demetrius briefly revived it in 302 BCE.

lukka.t: Lukka, a land of independent communities in south-western Anatolia, known as raiders and seafarers in Hittite and Egyptian texts.
lukka.o: The Lukka lands lay in the coastal mountains of south-western Anatolia, in later Lycia and Pisidia. Hittite records from the 15th century BCE show them as Luwian-speaking communities without a single king, outside or at the edge of Hittite authority.
lukka.r: Lukka people served the Hittite Empire as troops, fighting at Kadesh, and raided neighbours by sea; an Amarna letter from the king of Alashiya complains of their yearly attacks. They had no central government, which made them hard to control.
lukka.e: Lukka appear among the Sea Peoples who attacked Egypt under Merneptah in the late 13th century BCE. After the Hittite collapse their land became the heartland of the later Lycians, whose name continues theirs.

landgraviate-of-hesse-kassel.t: The largest of the Hessian landgraviates, known for hiring out its soldiers to Britain and for the Wilhelmshöhe palace above Kassel.
landgraviate-of-hesse-kassel.o: When Landgrave Philip the Magnanimous died in 1567, the Landgraviate of Hesse was divided among his four sons. William IV, the eldest, received about half, with Kassel as capital, and Hesse-Kassel later gained the northern part of Hesse-Marburg in 1604.
landgraviate-of-hesse-kassel.r: William IV was a noted astronomer, and Maurice the Learned adopted Calvinism and in 1605 built the Ottoneum, the first permanent theatre building in Germany. Landgravine Amalie Elisabeth held the land together in the Thirty Years' War. In the 18th century the landgraves hired out troops to Britain, including some 12,000 Hessians for the American War of Independence, paying for works such as the Hercules monument and Wilhelmshöhe.
landgraviate-of-hesse-kassel.e: In 1803 Landgrave William IX was made an elector, and Hesse-Kassel became the Electorate of Hesse. Napoleon absorbed it into the Kingdom of Westphalia in 1807; restored in 1813, the electorate was annexed by Prussia in 1866.

lordship-of-tyre.t: The Crusader lordship of Tyre, saved by Conrad of Montferrat in 1187 and later held by the Montfort family until the end of Outremer.
lordship-of-tyre.o: Tyre, taken by the Crusaders with Venetian help in 1124, was part of the royal domain of the Kingdom of Jerusalem. In 1187, when Saladin's victory left almost every other town lost, Conrad of Montferrat arrived and held Tyre against him, ruling it as his own base.
lordship-of-tyre.r: Tyre was the launching point of the Third Crusade and, with Acre, the kingdom's main port, with large Venetian and Genoese quarters. In the 1230s-1240s it was a stronghold of Frederick II's officials until the Ibelins took it in 1243. From 1246 Philip of Montfort held it as a lordship and built up its trade; he was killed by an Assassin in 1270.
lordship-of-tyre.e: His son John of Montfort and later heirs held it until 1291, when, after the fall of Acre, the Mamluks took Tyre without resistance.

lordship-of-pappenheim.t: The Franconian lordship of the hereditary imperial marshals of Pappenheim, a family famous for the cavalry general of the Thirty Years' War.
lordship-of-pappenheim.o: The lords of Pappenheim, ministerials of the Staufer, appear around 1141 in the Altmühl valley. They held the office of imperial marshal, later hereditary arch-marshal deputies to the Elector of Saxony, which gave the small family a prominent ceremonial role at coronations and diets.
lordship-of-pappenheim.r: The lordship around the castle and town of Pappenheim was small, but the family's members served emperors widely. Gottfried Heinrich of Pappenheim was a leading imperial cavalry commander in the Thirty Years' War, killed at Lützen in 1632. The family became counts in 1628. The town converted to Lutheranism.
lordship-of-pappenheim.e: Pappenheim was mediatised in 1806 and absorbed into the Kingdom of Bavaria, though the counts kept their castle and estates. The marshal office ended with the dissolution of the Empire in 1806.

livonian-order.t: Livonian branch of the Teutonic Order, which ruled most of medieval Latvia and Estonia and fought Russia and Lithuania for three centuries.
livonian-order.o: After the Livonian Brothers of the Sword were destroyed at Saule in 1236, the survivors were incorporated into the Teutonic Order in 1237, with Hermann Balk as first master in Livonia. The Order inherited the Sword Brothers' castles and lands and their role as the military power of Terra Mariana.
livonian-order.r: The Order's knights, mostly from Westphalia and the Rhineland, governed districts from stone castles under commanders and advocates, with headquarters at Riga and later Wenden (Cēsis). Defeats included Lake Peipus in 1242 against Alexander Nevsky and Durbe in 1260, but it conquered Courland and Semigallia and bought Danish Estonia in 1346. It fought long wars with the archbishops of Riga and with the city itself.
livonian-order.e: Master Wolter von Plettenberg defeated Muscovy at Smolina in 1502, but the Livonian War from 1558 was a disaster, with defeat at Ergeme in 1560. In 1561 the last master, Gotthard Kettler, secularised the Order's lands, becoming Duke of Courland and Semigallia under Polish-Lithuanian sovereignty.

lordship-of-pesaro.t: An Adriatic lordship held by the Malatesta and then the Sforza, before passing to the della Rovere dukes of Urbino in 1512.
lordship-of-pesaro.o: A branch of the Malatesta of Rimini took control of Pesaro in 1285 and ruled it as lords and papal vicars. In 1445 Galeazzo Malatesta sold Pesaro to Alessandro Sforza, brother of Francesco Sforza, who had married his granddaughter Costanza da Varano.
lordship-of-pesaro.r: Under the Malatesta and then the Sforza, Pesaro was a small Adriatic court state living from farming, fishing and maiolica pottery. Alessandro Sforza and his son Costanzo built the Rocca Costanza fortress and patronised artists. Giovanni Sforza, Costanzo's son, married Lucrezia Borgia, but the marriage was annulled and Cesare Borgia expelled him in 1500. He returned after Pope Alexander VI's death in 1503.
lordship-of-pesaro.e: After Giovanni's son died young, Pope Julius II granted Pesaro in 1512 to his nephew Francesco Maria I della Rovere, joining it to the Duchy of Urbino.

leontini.t: Inland Chalcidian city of eastern Sicily on a rich grain plain, whose envoy Gorgias drew Athens into Sicilian affairs in 427 BCE.
leontini.o: Thucydides records that Chalcidians from Naxos, led by Theocles, founded Leontini in 729 BCE, expelling the native Sicels from the site. It lay on hills above the Leontine plain, one of the most fertile grain-growing areas in Sicily, a short distance inland from the sea.
leontini.r: Leontini's wealth came from grain. Around 610 BCE Panaetius became the first known tyrant in Sicily there. The city fell under Hippocrates of Gela around 495 BCE and later under Syracuse. Under pressure from Syracuse it sent the orator Gorgias to Athens in 427 BCE, and his speeches won an Athenian alliance and the first Athenian expedition to Sicily; Gorgias also helped bring Sicilian rhetoric to Greece.
leontini.e: In 422 BCE the Leontine aristocrats expelled the common people and moved to Syracuse, which absorbed the city. Its plight was a pretext for the great Athenian expedition of 415 BCE. Leontini was later revived as a dependent town and as Lentini survives today.

lusitanians.t: The fierce Iron Age people of central Portugal whose leader Viriathus defeated Roman armies for years before his murder in 139 BCE.
lusitanians.o: The Lusitanians lived between the Douro and the Tagus, in central Portugal and the neighbouring parts of Extremadura, emerging as a recognisable people in the second half of the first millennium BCE. They spoke Lusitanian, an Indo-European language known from a handful of inscriptions in Latin letters, such as those of Cabeço das Fráguas.
lusitanians.r: Lusitanian society was organised in clans and hillfort communities, with warrior bands under chosen leaders and a herding and farming economy in the uplands. Raiding into the richer south was a constant feature. They worshipped local gods such as Bandua and Endovelicus, and their warriors fought in light, mobile formations that troubled Roman legions.
lusitanians.e: After raids from 155 BCE, the Roman praetor Galba massacred thousands under a false truce in 150 BCE. Viriathus, a survivor, led resistance until he was assassinated in 139 BCE, after which resistance collapsed. Their land later became the Roman province of Lusitania, a name later revived as a poetic name for Portugal.

lordship-of-dejanovic.t: Lordship of the Dejanović brothers in eastern Macedonia and western Bulgaria, Ottoman vassals whose daughter became a Byzantine empress.
lordship-of-dejanovic.o: The sebastokrator Dejan, a magnate and brother-in-law of Stefan Dušan, held lands around Kumanovo in the Serbian Empire. After Dušan's death his sons Jovan Dragaš and Konstantin Dragaš built an autonomous lordship stretching from Kumanovo to Velbazhd (Kyustendil) and Strumica.
lordship-of-dejanovic.r: The brothers ruled from Velbazhd and Strumica, taxing the trade routes between the Vardar and the Struma. After the Maritsa in 1371 they became Ottoman vassals, supplying troops. They endowed monasteries on Mount Athos and in Macedonia. Konstantin's daughter Helena married the Byzantine emperor Manuel II and was the mother of the last emperor, Constantine XI.
lordship-of-dejanovic.e: Jovan died around 1378. Konstantin was killed fighting as an Ottoman vassal at Rovine in 1395, and the Ottomans annexed his lands.

lordship-of-ramla.t: A lordship on the coastal plain of the Kingdom of Jerusalem that became a power base of the Ibelin family.
lordship-of-ramla.o: Ramla, the former capital of Fatimid Palestine, was occupied by the First Crusade in 1099. It was under royal control at first and became a lordship around 1120, held by a family whose heiress Helvis married Barisan of Ibelin, bringing it to the Ibelins.
lordship-of-ramla.r: Ramla and the nearby castle of Mirabel controlled the road from Jaffa to Jerusalem and rich farmland. The Ibelin lords Hugh and then Baldwin of Ibelin held it in the later 12th century; Baldwin was among the barons who fought at Montgisard nearby in 1177. In 1186 he refused to accept Guy of Lusignan as king and left for Antioch.
lordship-of-ramla.e: Ramla fell to Saladin in 1187. The title was revived but the lordship was never again held by the Franks in any lasting way.

lordship-of-biscay.t: A Basque lordship ruled by the Haro family under Navarre and Castile, whose fueros and assembly at Guernica made it a byword for local liberties.
lordship-of-biscay.o: Around 1040 Íñigo López Ezquerra appears in records as the first count or lord of Biscay, a vassal of Navarre. His descendants, the López de Haro, held the lordship for more than three centuries, moving their allegiance between Navarre and Castile.
lordship-of-biscay.r: The lords ruled with the consent of the Juntas Generales, the general assembly that met under the oak of Guernica and guarded Biscay's fueros, or customary laws. The economy depended on iron mining, forges, shipbuilding and fishing. In 1300 Lord Diego López V de Haro founded Bilbao, which grew into its chief port.
lordship-of-biscay.e: In 1379 the lordship passed by inheritance to John I of the Crown of Castile, and from then on the kings of Castile ruled Biscay as lords. Its fueros survived until the 19th century.

locri-epizephyrii.t: Greek city in Calabria famed for the law code of Zaleucus, the earliest written Greek laws, and for its sanctuary of Persephone.
locri-epizephyrii.o: Locrians from central Greece founded Locri Epizephyrii, 'Locri of the West Wind', around 680 BCE on the Ionian coast of Calabria, near Cape Zephyrion. Ancient writers said the settlers included slaves and women of noble families, a story that may reflect the status of women in the city's aristocracy.
locri-epizephyrii.r: Locri's laws, attributed to Zaleucus in the mid-7th century BCE, were reckoned the first written code in the Greek world and known for severe punishments. A council of a thousand governed the city. Its Persephone sanctuary yielded hundreds of painted terracotta plaques (pinakes). Locri defeated much larger Croton at the Sagras river and founded Hipponion and Medma. It was Syracuse's closest ally: Dionysius I married a Locrian woman, and Dionysius II ruled the city harshly from 356 to 346 BCE.
locri-epizephyrii.e: Locri became a Roman ally after the Pyrrhic War, went over to Hannibal and was retaken by Scipio in 205 BCE; the outrages of its commander Pleminius caused a scandal in Rome. It continued as a Roman town until abandoned in the early Middle Ages.

leuci.t: Gallic people of southern Lorraine around Toul, steady suppliers of grain to Caesar's armies.
leuci.o: The Leuci lived on the upper Moselle and Meuse, in the modern departments of Meurthe-et-Moselle and Vosges. Caesar mentions them among the peoples who supplied his army with grain in 58 BCE.
leuci.r: Nothing is known of their rulers. Their land included sanctuaries that grew important under Rome, above all Grand, a great healing shrine of Apollo Grannus with a large mosaic and amphitheatre.
leuci.e: The Leuci seem to have stayed loyal during the revolts, and Rome gave them the status of a free civitas. Their chief town Tullum became Toul, later one of the Three Bishoprics.

livonian-brothers-of-the-sword.t: Crusading military order founded in Riga in 1202, which conquered Livonia and Estonia before being destroyed at Saule in 1236.
livonian-brothers-of-the-sword.o: Bishop Albert of Riga and the Cistercian Theoderich founded the Brothers of the Sword in 1202 to provide a permanent army for the Livonian crusade, modelled on the Templars. Pope Innocent III approved it in 1204, and its knights wore a white mantle with a red sword and cross.
livonian-brothers-of-the-sword.r: The Order's knight-brothers, mostly from Saxony and Westphalia, lived under a monastic rule and governed conquered land from castles such as Wenden (Cēsis) and Fellin. The bishop granted them a third of conquered territory. Under masters Wenno and Volquin they subdued the Livs, Latgalians and Estonians, often quarrelling with the bishops and with Denmark over the spoils.
livonian-brothers-of-the-sword.e: In 1236 a crusade against Lithuania ended in disaster at the Battle of Saule, where Samogitians and Semigallians killed Master Volquin and about fifty brothers. The survivors were incorporated in 1237 into the Teutonic Order as its Livonian branch, the Livonian Order.

later-tang.t: The second of the Five Dynasties, founded by the Shatuo Turkic ruler Li Cunxu, who claimed to restore the Tang and briefly reunited much of northern China.
later-tang.o: Li Cunxu, ruler of Jin (Five Dynasties) at Taiyuan, proclaimed himself emperor of a restored Tang in 923 and within months captured Kaifeng, ending the Later Liang. He moved the capital to Luoyang, the old Tang eastern capital, and in 925 conquered Former Shu in Sichuan.
later-tang.r: The ruling house and much of its army were Shatuo Turks. Li Cunxu, a brilliant general, alienated his troops by favouring actors and was killed in a mutiny in 926. His adopted brother Li Siyuan (Emperor Mingzong) restored order, and under his minister Feng Dao work began in 932 on the first printed edition of the Confucian classics.
later-tang.e: After Mingzong's death, Li Congke seized the throne in 934. The governor Shi Jingtang rebelled at Taiyuan with Khitan help, promising them the Sixteen Prefectures. Li Congke burned himself to death in Luoyang as their armies arrived, and Shi Jingtang founded the Later Jin (936-947).

ligurian-republic.t: The French-sponsored republic that replaced the old Republic of Genoa in 1797 and was annexed to Napoleon's empire in 1805.
ligurian-republic.o: In May 1797 a democratic rising in Genoa, supported by France, overthrew the old aristocratic Republic of Genoa. By the Convention of Mombello in June 1797 Napoleon reorganised it as the Ligurian Republic, with a constitution on the French model.
ligurian-republic.r: The new republic abolished noble privilege, but the French controlled its policy and took its resources. In 1800 the Austrians and British besieged Genoa, held by General Masséna, causing terrible famine before the city surrendered shortly before Marengo restored French dominance. A new constitution of 1802 restored the title of doge, held by Girolamo Durazzo.
ligurian-republic.e: In June 1805 the Ligurian Republic was annexed to the French Empire. After Napoleon's fall the Republic of Genoa (1814) was briefly restored before Genoa passed to the Kingdom of Sardinia.

lombard-league.t: An alliance of northern Italian city-republics that defeated Frederick Barbarossa at Legnano in 1176 and won self-government from the emperors.
lombard-league.o: In 1167, according to tradition in an oath sworn at Pontida, Milan, Cremona, Bergamo, Brescia, Mantua and other cities formed a league against Frederick Barbarossa, absorbing the Veronese League. Pope Alexander III supported it, and the new city of Alessandria was named after him.
lombard-league.r: The league was an alliance of communes with a council of rectors from member cities, a shared war chest and joint armies, rather than a single state. Its forces defeated Barbarossa at Legnano in 1176, forcing the Truce of Venice in 1177 and the Peace of Constance in 1183, which recognised the cities' rights to elect their own officials.
lombard-league.e: The league was revived in 1226 against Frederick II, who defeated it at Cortenuova in 1237 but failed to break the cities. After Frederick's death in 1250 it faded away, as the communes turned to wars among themselves and to rule by lords.

lordship-of-ibelin.t: A small Crusader lordship whose castle gave its name to the Ibelins, the most powerful noble family of Outremer and Cyprus.
lordship-of-ibelin.o: In 1141 King Fulk built a castle at Yibna (Yavne), on the coastal plain south of Jaffa, as one of a ring of forts to contain the Fatimid garrison of Ascalon. He granted it to Barisan, constable of Jaffa, whose descendants took the name of Ibelin.
lordship-of-ibelin.r: The lordship itself was small, but the family rose quickly through marriage, gaining Ramla, Mirabel and Nablus. Barisan's sons Hugh, Baldwin and Balian of Ibelin were leading barons; Balian married the dowager queen Maria Komnene. The castle lost its military purpose after Ascalon fell in 1153.
lordship-of-ibelin.e: Ibelin was lost to Saladin in 1187, shortly after Balian negotiated the surrender of Jerusalem. The family survived the catastrophe and in the 13th century dominated Beirut, Jaffa, Arsuf and the Kingdom of Cyprus.

lahsa-eyalet.t: The Ottoman province of eastern Arabia, based at Hofuf, which guarded the Gulf flank of the empire for a century.
lahsa-eyalet.o: After the conquest of Iraq, the Ottoman Empire extended its reach down the Gulf coast and took al-Hasa around 1550, partly to counter the Portuguese. The province of Lahsa was organised around 1560 with its seat at Hofuf and included the port of Qatif.
lahsa-eyalet.r: Governors held the oasis towns with small garrisons of Janissaries and local levies, collecting taxes from the large date-growing oasis of al-Hasa and customs at Qatif. The province served as a base against Portuguese Bahrain, though an Ottoman expedition to take the island in 1559 failed. Control of the Bedouin hinterland was always weak, and governors were often isolated from Basra and Baghdad.
lahsa-eyalet.e: In 1670 the Bedouin chief Barrak ibn Ghurayr of the Banu Khalid expelled the Ottoman garrison and founded the Banu Khalid Emirate. The Ottomans returned to al-Hasa only in 1871.

lordship-of-verona.t: The Scaliger lordship that made Verona a power in north-eastern Italy, whose lord Cangrande della Scala sheltered Dante.
lordship-of-verona.o: After Ezzelino III da Romano died in 1259, the Commune of Verona chose Mastino I della Scala as its leader, and by 1262 he was effectively lord. His family, the della Scala or Scaligeri, made the office hereditary.
lordship-of-verona.r: The Scaligeri ruled Verona as lords and imperial vicars. Cangrande I, lord from 1311 to 1329, conquered Vicenza, Padua and Treviso and hosted the exiled Dante, who dedicated the Paradiso to him. Under Mastino II the lordship reached Lucca and Parma, but a coalition of Venice and Florence stripped most of it away in 1339. The family's Gothic tombs, the Arche Scaligere, and the Castelvecchio bridge survive.
lordship-of-verona.e: Family murders weakened the dynasty. In 1387 Gian Galeazzo Visconti seized Verona from Antonio della Scala and annexed it to the Lordship of Milan. Venice took the city in 1405.

lesser-nogai-horde.t: The western branch of the Nogai Horde, which moved to the Kuban steppe and became a client of the Crimean Khanate and the Ottomans.
lesser-nogai-horde.o: In 1557, amid a civil war within the Nogai Horde over relations with Russia, the mirza Kazy broke away with his followers and moved west across the Volga to the steppes of the North Caucasus and the Kuban. The new group became known as Kazy's Ulus or the Lesser Nogai Horde.
lesser-nogai-horde.r: The Lesser Nogais were pastoral nomads who raided Muscovite and Caucasian lands, often in alliance with the Crimean Khanate. They were ruled by mirzas of Kazy's line and recognised Crimean and, through it, Ottoman overlordship. Their horses and captives were traded through the Crimean ports.
lesser-nogai-horde.e: In the early 17th century many Lesser Nogais moved closer to the Crimean Khanate, especially after Kalmyk Khanate pressure in the 1630s. They were absorbed into the Crimean and Kuban Nogai communities, which were later annexed by Russia in 1783.

lordship-of-caesarea.t: A Crusader lordship on the coast of Palestine whose 13th-century walls still stand at Caesarea.
lordship-of-caesarea.o: Baldwin I took Caesarea in May 1101 with a Genoese fleet, which received a share of the spoils including a green glass bowl believed to be the Holy Grail, now the Sacro Catino in Genoa. The city became the seat of a lordship, held from about 1110 by Eustace Grenier and his descendants.
lordship-of-caesarea.r: Caesarea was one of the major lordships of the Kingdom of Jerusalem and the seat of a Latin archbishop. Its lords, the Grenier family and later the Aleman line, lived from the harbour and the coastal plain. The town was smaller than the Roman city, but its defences were rebuilt several times, most thoroughly by Louis IX in 1251-1252 with a sloping glacis and moat.
lordship-of-caesarea.e: Saladin took Caesarea in 1187; it was regained in 1191. In 1265 Baybars captured it after a short siege and razed its walls; John Aleman was its last lord.

lixus.t: An ancient Phoenician and Punic port on the Atlantic coast of Morocco, linked in Greek myth to the Garden of the Hesperides.
lixus.o: Lixus lay on a hill above the Loukkos river near modern Larache. Pliny the Elder believed it was among the oldest Phoenician foundations, with a temple of Melqart older than that of Gades. Archaeology shows Phoenician settlers there from about the 8th century BCE, trading with the Berber peoples of the interior.
lixus.r: Lixus was a self-governing town with Phoenician gods and Punic language, part of the trading world of the Punic Empire. Its economy rested on fishing, fish-salting and garum production, and it traded ivory, gold and grain along the Atlantic coast. Greek writers placed the Garden of the Hesperides and the struggle of Heracles with Antaeus nearby.
lixus.e: After the fall of Carthage Lixus came under the Kingdom of Mauretania, minting coins with Punic legends, and was fully absorbed under Juba II around 25 BCE. Claudius later made it a Roman colony, and its ruins, with large fish-salting works, are an archaeological site.

lordship-of-overijssel.t: The eastern Hanseatic lands of the former bishopric of Utrecht, with Deventer, Kampen and Zwolle, under Habsburg rule before joining the Dutch Republic.
lordship-of-overijssel.o: The Oversticht, the eastern part of the Prince-Bishopric of Utrecht, was ruled by the bishops until 1528, when Bishop Henry of Bavaria handed his temporal power to Charles V. Overijssel then became one of the Seventeen Provinces of the Habsburg Netherlands, with Drenthe attached to it.
lordship-of-overijssel.r: The province was governed by estates of nobles and the three towns of Deventer, Kampen and Zwolle, Hanseatic ports on the IJssel. Deventer was the birthplace of the Devotio Moderna movement and a centre of printing. The Habsburgs ruled through stadtholders but left the towns their privileges.
lordship-of-overijssel.e: Overijssel joined the Union of Utrecht in 1579 and, after the Act of Abjuration of 1581, the Dutch Republic, although Spanish troops held parts of it until the 1590s.

lordship-of-leo-sgouros.t: Short-lived domain of the Greek magnate Leo Sgouros in the north-eastern Peloponnese, the chief resistance to the Frankish conquest of southern Greece.
lordship-of-leo-sgouros.o: Leo Sgouros inherited power as archon of Nauplia from his father around 1198, as Byzantine authority weakened. He seized Argos and Corinth, attacked Athens and Thebes, and married Eudokia, daughter of the deposed emperor Alexios III, gaining a measure of legitimacy as Constantinople fell to the Fourth Crusade in 1204.
lordship-of-leo-sgouros.r: Sgouros ruled as an independent strongman from fortresses rather than through any formal state, using force and reputed cruelty, and dominating the Argolid, the Corinthia and the Isthmus. He tried to block Boniface of Montferrat at Thermopylae in 1204 but retreated to the near-impregnable citadel of Acrocorinth.
lordship-of-leo-sgouros.e: Besieged by the Franks, Sgouros died around 1208, reportedly riding his horse off the cliffs of Acrocorinth. Its garrison held out until about 1210, and Argos and Nauplia until 1212, when they fell to the Principality of Achaea and became the Lordship of Argos and Nauplia.

lipara.t: Greek city on the Aeolian Islands, founded by Cnidians, whose citizens shared land in common and fought Etruscan pirates at sea.
lipara.o: Settlers from Cnidus and Rhodes, led by the family of Pentathlus, settled on Lipari, the largest of the Aeolian Islands north of Sicily, around 580 BCE after failing to found a colony in western Sicily. The island had been inhabited since the Neolithic, when its obsidian was traded widely.
lipara.r: According to Diodorus, the Liparaeans at first held land in common, some farming while others manned the fleet against Etruscan pirates, and their victories were celebrated with dedications at Delphi. The city prospered from its harbour, alum and sea trade, and its necropolis has yielded fine pottery and theatre masks.
lipara.e: Lipara came under Carthaginian control in the 4th century BCE and served as a Carthaginian naval base in the First Punic War. Rome captured it in 252 BCE. It remained a town of Roman Sicily, today Lipari.

luluid-aleppo.t: A brief regime in Aleppo founded by the Hamdanid chamberlain Lu'lu', who displaced his masters and ruled with Fatimid recognition.
luluid-aleppo.o: Lu'lu' al-Kabir was a slave commander and chamberlain of the Hamdanids of Aleppo who had long been the real power behind the young emirs. In 1004 he deposed the last Hamdanid heirs and took power in his own name, recognising the Fatimid caliph in Cairo while keeping the Byzantine tribute arrangement.
luluid-aleppo.r: Lu'lu' and his son Mansur, who succeeded him around 1008, governed a small emirate squeezed between Byzantium and the Fatimids and threatened by the Bedouin Banu Kilab. Mansur tried to break the Kilab by treachery, imprisoning their leaders, among them Salih ibn Mirdas, who escaped.
luluid-aleppo.e: In 1016 the commander of the citadel, Fath al-Qal'i, handed Aleppo to the Fatimids, and Mansur fled to Byzantine territory. After a period of Fatimid governors, Salih ibn Mirdas took Aleppo in 1024 and founded the Mirdasid Emirate.

lordship-of-lesbos.t: Genoese lordship of the Gattilusi family on Lesbos, a Byzantine-allied dynasty that ruled northern Aegean islands until the Ottoman conquest in 1462.
lordship-of-lesbos.o: The Genoese adventurer Francesco Gattilusio helped the Byzantine emperor John V Palaiologos regain his throne in 1354. In reward John gave him his sister Maria in marriage and the island of Lesbos as a dowry in 1355, making the Gattilusi hereditary lords of the island, with Mytilene as their capital.
lordship-of-lesbos.r: The Gattilusi acted as Byzantine vassals and relatives, adopting Greek ways and titles, while trading with Genoa. Their family extended its power to Ainos, Thasos, Lemnos and Samothrace. They profited from alum, grain and the Black Sea trade, and from the 1390s paid tribute to the Ottomans. Mytilene's castle was rebuilt in their time.
lordship-of-lesbos.e: After the fall of Constantinople in 1453 the Gattilusi remained as Ottoman tributaries. In 1462 Mehmed II besieged and took Mytilene; the last lord, Niccolo Gattilusio, was taken to Constantinople and later executed.

lordship-of-milan.t: The signoria through which the Visconti turned Milan into the strongest state in northern Italy, before buying a ducal title in 1395.
lordship-of-milan.o: In 1259 Martino della Torre was made lord of the people, turning the Commune of Milan into a lordship. The della Torre were challenged by Archbishop Ottone Visconti, who defeated them at Desio in 1277; his great-nephew Matteo I Visconti received the title of imperial vicar in 1294.
lordship-of-milan.r: The Visconti ruled through councils and appointed podestà while keeping communal forms. Azzone Visconti absorbed Bergamo, Cremona, Como, Lodi, Brescia and other cities in the 1330s. Archbishop Giovanni Visconti added Genoa and Bologna, and in 1359 Galeazzo II took Pavia. Gian Galeazzo Visconti overthrew his uncle Bernabò in 1385 and created a centralised state, beginning Milan Cathedral in 1386.
lordship-of-milan.e: In 1395 Gian Galeazzo bought the title of duke from Emperor Wenceslas, turning the lordship into the Duchy of Milan, which he expanded towards Tuscany and Umbria before his death in 1402.

lordship-of-faenza.t: The Manfredi lordship of Faenza in Romagna, the town whose glazed pottery gave Europe the word 'faience'.
lordship-of-faenza.o: The Manfredi family led Faenza's Guelphs in the 13th century, and in 1313 Francesco Manfredi became lord of the city. The family ruled as papal vicars, though they lost and regained the city several times in the 14th century.
lordship-of-faenza.r: The Manfredi governed Faenza and neighbouring towns such as Imola for a time, often serving as condottieri for Florence, Milan or Venice. The town's maiolica workshops flourished in the 15th century, and their glazed earthenware gave French and English the name faience. Carlo II Manfredi rebuilt the cathedral and the town centre in Renaissance style.
lordship-of-faenza.e: In 1501 Cesare Borgia besieged Faenza, which surrendered; the young lord Astorre III Manfredi was taken to Rome and murdered in 1502. Venice held Faenza until 1509, when it passed to the Papal States.
