landgraviate-of-thuringia.t: The principality of the Ludowingian landgraves at the Wartburg, a centre of courtly poetry and the home of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary.
landgraviate-of-thuringia.o: The Ludowingian family, founded by Louis the Bearded, built up lands in Thuringia in the 11th century, building the Wartburg near Eisenach around 1067. In 1131 Emperor Lothair III raised Louis I to landgrave, giving him comital rights over Thuringia, and in 1180 they also gained the County Palatine of Saxony.
landgraviate-of-thuringia.r: Landgrave Hermann I made the Wartburg a centre of Minnesang, hosting poets such as Walther von der Vogelweide and Wolfram von Eschenbach; this was later remembered as the Wartburg contest of song. His son Louis IV married Elizabeth of Hungary, canonised in 1235 for her charity. The landgraves governed from Eisenach and the Wartburg.
landgraviate-of-thuringia.e: After the Ludowingians died out with Henry Raspe in 1247, the War of the Thuringian Succession gave Thuringia to the Wettin Henry the Illustrious of Meissen in 1264, while Hesse broke away. The landgraviate merged with Wettin lands, ending as a separate unit in 1440.

lobedu-kingdom.t: The Limpopo kingdom of the Rain Queens, the Modjadji, whose rainmaking power was respected far beyond its small territory.
lobedu-kingdom.o: Lobedu tradition traces the royal line to a princess who fled from the Karanga lands of present-day Zimbabwe with rain medicines, settling in the Molototsi valley in the north-eastern Transvaal by the 17th century. The kingdom was ruled by kings until around 1800, when the first queen, Maselekwane Modjadji I, came to power.
lobedu-kingdom.r: The Rain Queen ruled through district heads and councillors and was believed to control rain. She did not marry but received wives from subject districts, and her daughters by them formed political ties across the kingdom. Rulers as distant as the Zulu and Swazi kings sent gifts to seek rain, and the Lobedu were spared by many invaders.
lobedu-kingdom.e: The kingdom resisted Transvaal Boer authority until a campaign in 1894 brought it under the South African Republic. The Rain Queen survived as a traditional office, and the Lobedu inspired H. Rider Haggard's novel She.

lebanese-republic.t: The republic of Lebanon, founded under French mandate in 1926, whose sharing of power among religious communities defines its politics.
lebanese-republic.o: On 23 May 1926 the constitution adopted by the representative council turned Greater Lebanon into the Lebanese Republic, with Charles Debbas as first president, still under the French Mandate for Syria and the Lebanon.
lebanese-republic.r: The unwritten National Pact of 1943, agreed by Bechara El Khoury and Riad Al Solh, reserved the presidency for a Maronite, the premiership for a Sunni and the speakership for a Shia. Independence was won in November 1943. Beirut became a banking, trade and cultural centre, but sectarian and social tensions, the 1958 crisis and the presence of Palestinian armed groups led to the civil war of 1975-1990.
lebanese-republic.e: The Taif Agreement of 1989 ended the war, though Syrian troops stayed until 2005, leaving after the assassination of Rafic Hariri. Lebanon then suffered the 2006 war, the 2019 financial collapse, the 2020 Beirut port explosion and the 2024 war between Israel and Hezbollah; Joseph Aoun became president in 2025.
lebanese-republic.re: Christianity, Sunni and Shia Islam, Druze

lordship-of-cortona.t: The Casali family's lordship over the Tuscan hill town of Cortona, which ended when the king of Naples sold it to Florence.
lordship-of-cortona.o: Cortona, an Etruscan hill town above the Valdichiana, had long been a self-governing commune and gained its own bishop in 1325. That year Ranieri Casali, head of a leading local family, became lord of the city, which the Casali then ruled as a hereditary lordship.
lordship-of-cortona.r: The Casali governed a small territory of hill and plain between Arezzo, Siena and Perugia, balancing between these neighbours and seeking imperial and papal recognition. Family murders over the succession were common. Little is known of their administration beyond the town's walls and the fortress they built.
lordship-of-cortona.e: In 1409 King Ladislaus of Naples captured Cortona from the last Casali lord during his wars in central Italy. In 1411 he sold the town to the Republic of Florence.

league-of-prizren.t: Albanian political and military league formed in 1878 to defend Albanian-inhabited lands from partition, and the starting point of the Albanian national movement.
league-of-prizren.o: The treaties of San Stefano and Berlin in 1878 assigned Albanian-inhabited districts to Montenegro, Serbia and Greece. On 10 June 1878 Albanian notables met in Prizren and formed a league to resist the partition, at first with tacit Ottoman approval, under leaders such as Ymer Prizreni, Abdyl Frashëri and Sulejman Vokshi.
league-of-prizren.r: The league raised armed volunteers and set up local committees, mainly among Muslim landowners and highland clans, though Catholic Albanians also took part. It fought Montenegro over Plav and Gusinje and Ulcinj. Under Abdyl Frashëri it moved from defending Ottoman territory to demanding a single autonomous Albanian province, and in 1880 it took over administration in Kosovo.
league-of-prizren.e: Alarmed by the league's autonomy demands and under European pressure, the Ottoman government sent Dervish Pasha's army, which crushed it in 1881. Its leaders were imprisoned or exiled, but its programme inspired Albanian nationalists until independence in 1912.

lordship-of-mecklenburg.t: The Christian lordship founded by the Obotrite prince Pribislav, whose dynasty ruled Mecklenburg from 1167 to 1918.
lordship-of-mecklenburg.o: After Henry the Lion's campaigns destroyed Obotrite power and killed Prince Niklot in 1160, his son Pribislav accepted Christianity and Saxon overlordship. In 1167 Henry restored most of his father's lands to him, except the County of Schwerin. Pribislav's descendants took their title from the old stronghold of Mecklenburg near Wismar.
lordship-of-mecklenburg.r: The lords encouraged German settlement, founding towns such as Rostock, Wismar and Güstrow, several of which joined the Hanseatic League. Doberan Abbey, founded in 1171, became the family burial place. After 1229 the lands divided into Mecklenburg, Werle, Rostock and Parchim-Richenberg, each with its own branch.
lordship-of-mecklenburg.e: In 1348 Emperor Charles IV raised Albert II of Mecklenburg to duke. His son Albert became King of Sweden in 1364. Mecklenburg remained ruled by the same dynasty, divided into Mecklenburg-Schwerin and Mecklenburg-Strelitz, until 1918, the only Slavic-origin ruling house in Germany.

lordship-of-schellenberg.t: A small Rhine-valley lordship that the princes of Liechtenstein bought in 1699 and joined with Vaduz to create their principality.
lordship-of-schellenberg.o: The lordship took its name from the Schellenberg family, Bavarian ministeriales who settled in the Rhine valley in the 13th century and built castles on the Eschnerberg ridge. After they sold their rights in the early 14th century, the lordship passed to other houses, among them the barons of Brandis, the counts of Sulz and the County of Hohenems.
lordship-of-schellenberg.r: Schellenberg was a rural district of a few villages, including Eschen, Mauren and Gamprin, ruled by distant lords through a bailiff. Its peasants lived from farming and livestock and kept local assemblies. It was usually held together with the neighbouring County of Vaduz, and both were direct fiefs of the empire, a status that later proved valuable.
lordship-of-schellenberg.e: The heavily indebted counts of Hohenems sold Schellenberg in 1699 to Prince Johann Adam Andreas of Liechtenstein, who wanted an imperial territory to win a seat in the Imperial Diet. In 1719 Emperor Charles VI united Schellenberg and Vaduz as the Principality of Liechtenstein, where it survives as the Unterland.

landgraviate-of-hesse.t: Central German landgraviate that broke away from Thuringia in 1264 and, under Philip the Magnanimous, became a leading Protestant power.
landgraviate-of-hesse.o: When the Ludowingian landgraves of Thuringia died out in 1247, Sophie of Brabant fought the Wettins in the War of the Thuringian Succession to secure Hesse for her son Henry I the Child. The settlement of 1264 separated Hesse from Thuringia, and in 1292 Henry was made an imperial prince.
landgraviate-of-hesse.r: The landgraves ruled from Marburg and Kassel, expanding by acquiring the County of Katzenelnbogen in 1479. Philip I the Magnanimous introduced the Reformation in 1526, founded the University of Marburg in 1527, hosted the Marburg Colloquy between Luther and Zwingli in 1529 and co-led the Schmalkaldic League. His bigamous second marriage weakened the Protestant cause.
landgraviate-of-hesse.e: After Philip's death in 1567, Hesse was divided among his four sons into Hesse-Kassel, Hesse-Marburg, Hesse-Rheinfels and Hesse-Darmstadt. Kassel and Darmstadt became the main successors, later the Electorate of Hesse and the Grand Duchy of Hesse.

liao-dynasty.t: The empire of the Khitan people, which ruled Mongolia, Manchuria and the far north of China for two centuries and gave China its medieval name, Cathay.
liao-dynasty.o: Abaoji of the Yila clan united the Khitan tribes of the Liao river basin and in 916 proclaimed himself emperor. In 926 he destroyed Balhae, setting up the client kingdom of Dongdan. His son Yelü Deguang gained the Sixteen Prefectures around modern Beijing from Later Jin (936-947) in 938 and adopted the dynastic name Liao in 947.
liao-dynasty.r: Liao governed with a dual system: a Northern Administration for the Khitan and other nomads under tribal law, and a Southern Administration on Tang lines for Chinese farmers. It had five capitals, two Khitan scripts created in the 920s, and a court that migrated between seasonal camps. Buddhism flourished, as the wooden pagoda at Yingxian shows. The Treaty of Chanyuan of 1005 brought annual payments of silver and silk from the Song Dynasty.
liao-dynasty.e: The Jurchen under Aguda rebelled in 1114 and founded the Jin dynasty (1115-1234), which captured the last emperor, Tianzuo, in 1125. Yelü Dashi led survivors west to found the Qara Khitai.

lordship-of-toron.t: A Crusader lordship in the hills of southern Lebanon whose lords, the Humphreys of Toron, were among the great barons of Jerusalem.
lordship-of-toron.o: Around 1105 Hugh of Saint-Omer, lord of the Principality of Galilee, built the castle of Toron at Tibnin in the hills above Tyre to support raids on the city, which was still in Muslim hands. It became a lordship held by the Toron family.
lordship-of-toron.r: Humphrey II of Toron was constable of the kingdom and a respected negotiator with the Muslims. His grandson Humphrey IV married Isabella, heir to the throne, but refused to be made king in 1186 and later lost her when barons forced their divorce. The lordship controlled hill villages and the routes from Tyre to Banyas.
lordship-of-toron.e: Saladin took Toron in 1187, and German crusaders failed to retake it in 1197-1198. It was returned by the treaty of 1229 and passed to the Montfort family, but Baybars captured it in 1266. The castle site is still occupied by a later fortress in Tibnin.

lordship-of-forli.t: The Ordelaffi lordship of Forlì in Romagna, a Ghibelline house that hosted Dante and long defied papal armies.
lordship-of-forli.o: The Ordelaffi family led Forlì's Ghibellines, and in 1315 they became lords of the city. They ruled, sometimes as papal vicars and sometimes in open rebellion, over Forlì and at times Cesena and other Romagna towns.
lordship-of-forli.r: Scarpetta Ordelaffi hosted the exiled Dante around 1303. Francesco II Ordelaffi resisted Cardinal Albornoz's campaign to restore papal rule for years; his wife Cia degli Ubaldini defended Cesena in 1357 until forced to surrender, and Forlì fell in 1359. The family regained the city in 1376. Forlì lived from farming the Romagna plain and from the condottiere careers of its lords.
lordship-of-forli.e: Pino III Ordelaffi died in 1480, and Pope Sixtus IV granted Forlì to his nephew Girolamo Riario, joining it to the Lordship of Imola and Forli.

landgraviate-of-hesse-darmstadt.t: The youngest of the Hessian landgraviates, ruled from Darmstadt, which grew into the Grand Duchy of Hesse.
landgraviate-of-hesse-darmstadt.o: The 1567 division of the Landgraviate of Hesse gave George I, youngest son of Philip the Magnanimous, the Upper County of Katzenelnbogen, about an eighth of the land, with Darmstadt as capital. Shares of Hesse-Rheinfels in 1583 and of Hesse-Marburg in 1604 enlarged it.
landgraviate-of-hesse-darmstadt.r: The landgraves remained Lutheran and loyal to the emperor, unlike Calvinist Kassel. Louis V founded the University of Giessen in 1607, and in 1622 a cadet line was established as the Landgraviate of Hesse-Homburg. The landgraves inherited the County of Hanau-Lichtenberg in 1736, and Landgravine Caroline made the Darmstadt court a meeting place for writers, including Goethe and Herder.
landgraviate-of-hesse-darmstadt.e: Allied with Napoleon, Landgrave Louis X joined the Confederation of the Rhine in 1806 and became Grand Duke Louis I of the Grand Duchy of Hesse, which lasted until 1918.

lordship-of-albarracin.t: A tiny independent Christian lordship in the mountains of Teruel, whose Azagra lords refused to be vassals of either Castile or Aragon.
lordship-of-albarracin.o: Around 1170 the Navarrese noble Pedro Ruiz de Azagra obtained Albarracín from Ibn Mardanish of the Second Taifa of Murcia, whom he had served. He resettled the town with Christians and declared that he held it as a vassal of the Virgin Mary alone.
lordship-of-albarracin.r: The lords of Albarracín ruled a mountain territory of pasture and forest, granted a fuero to settlers and created a bishopric. Their autonomy rested on balancing between the Crown of Castile and the Crown of Aragon, and the family kept it for over a century.
lordship-of-albarracin.e: The lordship passed by marriage to Juan Núñez de Lara. In 1284 Peter III of Aragon besieged and captured Albarracín, and it was incorporated into the Kingdom of Aragon in 1300.

lindos.t: The greatest of the three old cities of Rhodes, crowned by the sanctuary of Athena Lindia and ruled by the sage Cleobulus.
lindos.o: Dorian Greeks settled Rhodes in the early Iron Age, forming three cities, Lindos, Ialysos and Kamiros. Lindos, on the east coast with the island's best natural harbours, grew around its acropolis sanctuary of Athena, and joined the Dorian Hexapolis with Knidos, Kos and Halicarnassus.
lindos.r: Lindian sailors founded Gela in Sicily with Cretans in 688 BCE and traded with Egypt and the Levant. In the 6th century BCE Cleobulus, counted among the Seven Sages, ruled as tyrant and rebuilt the temple of Athena. Lindos later fell under the Achaemenid Empire and then belonged to the Delian League.
lindos.e: In 408 BCE Lindos joined Ialysos and Kamiros to found the new city of Rhodes, which became the island's capital. Lindos remained a religious centre: the Lindian Chronicle of 99 BCE lists famous offerings to Athena, and the acropolis is still a landmark.
lindos.re: Greek religion; cult of Athena Lindia

lakhmid-kingdom.t: The Arab client kingdom of the Sasanians at al-Hira, a centre of early Arabic poetry and Christianity on the Euphrates.
lakhmid-kingdom.o: The Lakhmids, or Nasrids, established themselves at al-Hira near the Euphrates in the late 3rd century as allies of the Sasanian Empire. The Namara inscription of 328 commemorates Imru al-Qays, son of Amr, as king of all the Arabs; he is usually counted as an early Lakhmid ruler.
lakhmid-kingdom.r: From al-Hira the kings controlled the Arab tribes of the desert fringe for Persia and fought the Ghassanid Kingdom on Byzantium's behalf. al-Mundhir III raided Syria repeatedly in the 6th century. al-Hira was a cosmopolitan town with a large Church of the East community, monasteries and a court that drew poets such as Tarafa and al-Nabigha, helping shape classical Arabic.
lakhmid-kingdom.e: In 602 Khosrow II deposed and executed al-Nu'man III, the last Lakhmid king, and replaced the dynasty with Persian governors. The loss of this buffer contributed to the Arab victory over Persian forces at Dhi Qar and left the frontier open to the armies of the Rashidun Caliphate, which took al-Hira in 633.
lakhmid-kingdom.re: Arabian polytheism, later Church of the East

lingones.t: Gallic people of the Langres plateau around the sources of the Seine and Marne, who stayed loyal to Rome during the great revolt of 52 BCE.
lingones.o: The Lingones held the uplands around Andematunnum (Langres), between the Sequani, the Aedui and the Leuci, astride the watershed between the Seine and Saône basins. Livy and Polybius record that part of the people joined the Celtic migrations into Italy around 400 BCE and settled near the Adriatic coast south of the Po.
lingones.r: Like their neighbours they lived in fortified oppida, struck their own coins and profited from the routes linking the Saône with the Seine. Little is known of their institutions, but they were large enough to supply Caesar's armies with grain.
lingones.e: The Lingones refused to join Vercingetorix in 52 BCE and were rewarded with the status of an allied civitas under Rome. In 70 CE their nobleman Julius Sabinus joined the revolt of the Batavi and proclaimed himself Caesar; after its failure his wife Epponina hid him for nine years before both were executed.

lordship-of-padua.t: The Carrara lordship of Padua, patrons of Petrarch and rivals of Venice, whose last lords were strangled in a Venetian prison.
lordship-of-padua.o: Threatened by Cangrande della Scala, the Commune of Padua in 1318 elected Jacopo I da Carrara as its lord. The Carrara lost Padua to the Lordship of Verona from 1328 to 1337 but then returned, ruling as hereditary lords.
lordship-of-padua.r: The Carraresi governed from the Reggia Carrarese palace and controlled Padua's university, which flourished. Francesco I, called the Elder, ruled from 1350, welcomed Petrarch and expanded the state towards Treviso and Friuli, making him a rival of Venice. Giusto de' Menabuoi frescoed the baptistery for the family. Gian Galeazzo Visconti took Padua in 1388, but Francesco Novello regained it in 1390.
lordship-of-padua.e: After a long war, the Republic of Venice captured Padua in 1405. Francesco Novello and two of his sons were strangled in prison in Venice in 1406, and Padua remained Venetian until 1797.

luash.t: Lu'ash, an Iron Age kingdom of inner Syria centred on Hatarikka, united with Hamath under King Zakkur.
luash.o: Lu'ash occupied the land between Hamath and Aleppo, the former Nuhashshe of the Bronze Age. Its capital Hatarikka, the biblical Hadrach, is identified with Tell Afis. It emerged as an Aramaean kingdom in the 9th century BCE.
luash.r: Around 800 BCE Zakkur, king of Hamath and Lu'ash, was besieged in Hatarikka by a coalition led by Bar-Hadad of Aram-Damascus. His Aramaic stele, found at Tell Afis, thanks the god Baalshamin for deliverance. The kingdom lived from grain farming and the routes of inner Syria.
luash.e: Tiglath-Pileser III of the Assyrian Empire annexed Lu'ash in 738 BCE, making Hatarikka the capital of a province.

lordship-of-frisia.t: Friesland west of the Ems under foreign lords after the end of the Frisian Freedom, passing from Saxony to Charles V and then into the Dutch Revolt.
lordship-of-frisia.o: In 1498 Emperor Maximilian named Albert of Saxony hereditary governor of Friesland, ending the Frisian Freedom west of the Ems. Saxon troops imposed their rule with difficulty against Frisian resistance and the city of Groningen.
lordship-of-frisia.r: Saxon government brought new courts and taxes, resented by many Frisians. Charles of Egmond of Guelders encouraged revolt, and the rebel leader Grutte Pier raided the coasts in the 1510s. George of Saxony sold his rights to the future Charles V in 1515, and from 1524 Habsburg stadtholders ruled from Leeuwarden with a new court of justice, the Hof van Friesland.
lordship-of-frisia.e: Friesland joined the Revolt against Philip II, signed the Union of Utrecht in 1580, and after the Act of Abjuration of 1581 became a province of the Dutch Republic, with its own stadtholders from the Nassau family.

lordship-of-glamorgan.t: The largest of the Welsh marcher lordships, seized from the last Welsh king of Morgannwg by Robert Fitzhamon and ruled from Cardiff Castle.
lordship-of-glamorgan.o: Around 1093 Robert Fitzhamon overthrew Iestyn ap Gwrgant of the Kingdom of Morgannwg and built a castle at Cardiff inside the old Roman fort. He granted manors in the fertile Vale of Glamorgan to his knights, while Welsh lords kept the uplands.
lordship-of-glamorgan.r: Glamorgan was a marcher lordship, held outside the ordinary English shire system with its own courts and military power. Through inheritance it passed to the earls of Gloucester, notably the Clare family, who built the vast Caerphilly Castle in the 1260s against Llywelyn ap Gruffudd. It later passed to the Despensers, Beauchamps and Nevilles.
lordship-of-glamorgan.e: The Laws in Wales Act of 1536 abolished the marcher lordships, and Glamorgan became a shire of the Kingdom of England, with Cardiff its county town.

league-of-the-ten-jurisdictions.t: The youngest of the Three Leagues of the Grisons, formed at Davos in 1436 when the last count of Toggenburg died without heirs.
league-of-the-ten-jurisdictions.o: When Frederick VII, last count of the County of Toggenburg, died in 1436, the ten court districts (Gerichte) he had held in the Prättigau, around Davos and in the Schanfigg formed a league at Davos to keep their rights and unity. Their lords remained, but the communes now acted together.
league-of-the-ten-jurisdictions.r: The league joined self-governing communes, each with its own court and assembly, and met at Davos. The Habsburgs later acquired lordship over eight of the jurisdictions, causing friction until the communes bought out those rights between 1649 and 1652. The league allied with the League of God's House in 1450 and the Grey League in 1471, forming the Three Leagues. Most communes became Reformed.
league-of-the-ten-jurisdictions.e: The league ended with the Three Leagues when the Grisons were attached to the Helvetic Republic in 1799, and it became part of the canton of Graubünden in 1803.

landgraviate-of-leuchtenberg.t: Upper Palatinate landgraviate whose Catholic landgraves ruled from Pfreimd until 1646, a title later revived for Napoleon's stepson Eugène de Beauharnais.
landgraviate-of-leuchtenberg.o: The lords of Leuchtenberg held a castle above the Naab valley in the Upper Palatinate and rose in the late 12th century, receiving the rank of landgrave in the 1190s. Their title gave them an unusual dignity for a modest territory between the Wittelsbach lands and Bohemia.
landgraviate-of-leuchtenberg.r: The landgraves ruled a small, rural territory and from 1332 resided at Pfreimd, where they later built a palace. They served the emperors and the Bohemian kings and sold or pledged lands to Bohemia and the Palatinate, so their domain shrank. The house remained Catholic during the Reformation, while much of the surrounding Upper Palatinate turned Protestant.
landgraviate-of-leuchtenberg.e: The last landgrave, Maximilian Adam, died in 1646, and Leuchtenberg passed to Bavaria. In 1817 the King of Bavaria created the title Duke of Leuchtenberg for Eugène de Beauharnais, whose descendants married into the Swedish, Portuguese and Russian royal families.

lordship-of-leinster.t: The vast Anglo-Norman liberty in south-east Ireland won by Strongbow, whose division in 1247 created the counties of Leinster.
lordship-of-leinster.o: Diarmait Mac Murchada, deposed king of Leinster, sought Norman help and promised his daughter Aoife and succession to Richard de Clare, Strongbow. After Diarmait's death in 1171 Strongbow claimed Leinster, and Henry II granted it to him as a lordship under the crown in the Lordship of Ireland.
lordship-of-leinster.r: Strongbow and his successors settled knights, founded towns and built castles such as Kilkenny and Ferns. William Marshal, who married Strongbow's daughter Isabel, developed New Ross, Kilkenny and many abbeys, and granted Kilkenny its charter. The lordship had its own courts, exchequer and seneschal.
lordship-of-leinster.e: The five sons of William Marshal all died without heirs, and in 1247 the liberty was divided among his daughters' heirs, forming Carlow, Kilkenny, Wexford, Kildare and part of Laois. The Butler earls of Ormond later held much of it.

lordship-of-the-isles.t: The MacDonald sea lordship of the Hebrides and western Highlands, a Gaelic power so strong its lords negotiated with England as near-independent princes.
lordship-of-the-isles.o: John of Islay, a descendant of Somerled of the Kingdom of Argyll and the Isles, styled himself Dominus Insularum, Lord of the Isles, from 1336. Through marriage and royal favour he united most of the Hebrides and much of the western mainland under Clan Donald.
lordship-of-the-isles.r: The lords held council at Finlaggan on Islay, with a council of the isles, and patronised the Iona abbey, galley-building, Gaelic poets and physicians. Donald of the Isles fought the Battle of Harlaw in 1411 over the earldom of Ross. John MacDonald II's secret Treaty of Westminster-Ardtornish with Edward IV in 1462 planned to partition Scotland.
lordship-of-the-isles.e: When the treaty was discovered, John lost Ross in 1475. In 1493 James IV forfeited the lordship, and the title was later annexed to the heir of the Scottish crown in the Kingdom of Scotland.

lucanians.t: Oscan-speaking people who took over much of southern Italy in the 5th and 4th centuries BCE, conquering Greek Poseidonia and defeating Thurii.
lucanians.o: The Lucanians formed in the 5th century BCE from Samnite groups moving south into the mountains of modern Basilicata and the Cilento. They absorbed or displaced earlier peoples, the Oenotrians and Chones, and pressed the Greek cities of the coast, capturing Poseidonia around 410 BCE.
lucanians.r: They lived in fortified hill settlements such as Serra di Vaglio and Roccagloriosa, and were led in war by elected kings. Their federal sanctuary of the goddess Mefitis at Rossano di Vaglio has yielded Oscan inscriptions in Greek letters. Painted tombs at Paestum show armoured horsemen and funeral games. They defeated Thurii near Laus in 389 BCE and killed Alexander of Epirus at Pandosia in 331 BCE.
lucanians.e: The Bruttii broke away from them in 356 BCE. The Lucanians allied with Rome in 298 BCE, then turned against it with Pyrrhus and were subdued by 272 BCE. They later backed Hannibal and the Social War rebels, and their region became the Roman Lucania.

land-of-punt.t: A fabled land of incense, ebony and gold on the southern Red Sea, reached by Egyptian trading fleets for over a thousand years.
land-of-punt.o: Punt is known almost entirely from Egyptian sources. The earliest recorded expedition went out under Sahure of the 5th Dynasty, c. 2450 BCE, and later voyages sailed from Red Sea harbours such as Mersa Gawasis. Its exact location is still debated, with proposals ranging from eastern Sudan and Eritrea to the Somali coast, while recent isotope studies of baboon mummies point to the Eritrea and Ethiopia region.
land-of-punt.r: Egyptians prized Punt for myrrh and frankincense, ebony, ivory, gold, leopard skins and live baboons. The best-known record, the reliefs of Hatshepsut's temple at Deir el-Bahari (c. 1470 BCE), show houses on stilts, domed huts, a ruler called Parahu and his queen Ati, and myrrh trees being loaded in baskets for replanting in Egypt. Nothing is known of its own language or institutions.
land-of-punt.e: References fade after the New Kingdom, with the last expeditions recorded under Ramesses III in the 12th century BCE. Punt survived in Egyptian memory as a semi-mythical 'God's Land', and some historians see it as a forerunner of the trade networks later dominated by D'mt and the Kingdom of Aksum.

lobetani.t: An obscure Iberian or Celtiberian people of the Teruel highlands, known almost only from the geographer Ptolemy.
lobetani.o: The Lobetani are recorded mainly by Ptolemy in the 2nd century CE, who places them in the mountains of eastern Spain with a town called Lobeton, perhaps near Albarracín in modern Teruel. Their origin and language are unknown.
lobetani.r: Nothing is known of their society beyond a probable highland economy of herding, and archaeology cannot securely identify their settlements.
lobetani.e: Their territory was absorbed into Hispania Citerior during the Roman conquest of the interior in the 2nd century BCE. They are remembered only as a name in the ancient geographies.

league-of-lezhe.t: Alliance of Albanian lords under Skanderbeg that resisted the Ottoman Empire for a quarter of a century and became a symbol of Albanian unity.
league-of-lezhe.o: On 2 March 1444, in the Venetian-held town of Lezhë, Skanderbeg gathered the leading Albanian nobles, among them the Arianiti, Dukagjini, Muzaka, Thopia, Zaharia and Balšić families and Stefan Crnojević of Zeta. They agreed to pool troops and revenues under his command against the Ottomans, with Krujë as the centre of resistance.
league-of-lezhe.r: The league was a military alliance rather than a unified state: each lord kept his own lands, while Skanderbeg led a mobile army that used mountain terrain to defeat larger Ottoman forces, as at Torvioll in 1444 and Albulena in 1457. Krujë withstood Ottoman sieges in 1450, 1466 and 1467. Skanderbeg sought support from Naples, Venice and the papacy.
league-of-lezhe.e: The alliance frayed early, through a war with Venice in 1447 and defections of lords. After Skanderbeg died at Lezhë in 1468, Lekë Dukagjini and Venice fought on, but Krujë fell in 1478 and Shkodër in 1479. Skanderbeg's flag and memory became central to Albanian nationalism.

liburnians.t: Seafaring Illyrian people of the northern Dalmatian coast and islands whose fast galley, the liburna, was copied by the Roman navy.
liburnians.o: The Liburnians appear in Greek sources by the 8th century BCE, holding the coast and islands between the Raša and Krka rivers in modern Croatia. Iron Age hillforts and cemeteries such as Nin show a distinct culture already formed, with wide maritime contacts. Before Corinthian settlers took Corcyra in 733 BCE, Liburnians are said to have held the island.
liburnians.r: They lived in fortified hill settlements grouped around centres such as Iader (Zadar), Aenona (Nin) and Scardona, with no single king recorded. Sea trade and raiding made them a power on the Adriatic, and their light two-banked galley became a standard warship. Greek writers claimed women held unusual authority among them. Amber and Italian goods passed through their ports.
liburnians.e: Greek colonies such as Issa and the rise of the Illyrian Kingdom cut back their sea power. They came under Roman control in the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE and were finally subdued during Octavian's Illyrian campaign of 35 BCE. Their towns became Roman municipia in Dalmatia.

leucas.t: Corinthian colony on the Ionian island of Lefkada, which cut a canal through its isthmus and later became the capital of the Acarnanian League.
leucas.o: Corinthians led by a son of the tyrant Cypselus founded Leucas c. 640 BCE on what was then a peninsula of Acarnania. The colonists dug a canal through the isthmus, making it an island. Its white cliffs at Cape Leucatas were linked with the legend of Sappho's leap.
leucas.r: Leucas stayed close to Corinth, fighting at Salamis in 480 BCE and with Corinth at Sybota in 433 BCE, and was a member of the Peloponnesian League. It was an oligarchy living from trade along the route to Italy. In the Hellenistic period it joined the Acarnanian League and became its meeting place.
leucas.e: After the Third Macedonian War Rome separated Leucas from Acarnania in 167 BCE, and it came under Roman control. The island is today's Lefkada.
leucas.re: Greek religion; cult of Apollo Leucatas

lexovii.t: Gallic people of the Pays d'Auge in Normandy, whose name survives in the town of Lisieux.
lexovii.o: The Lexovii lived between the Seine estuary and the Orne, with a coastline on the Channel. Caesar names them among the peoples of the Atlantic seaboard.
lexovii.r: Caesar records that in 56 BCE they killed their senators, who would not support war, and joined the coalition of Viridovix, showing a council of nobles similar to those of their neighbours.
lexovii.e: Defeated by Quintus Titurius Sabinus in 56 BCE, they also sent troops to Alesia in 52 BCE. Under Rome their chief town was Noviomagus Lexoviorum, the origin of Lisieux, later a bishopric.

lordship-of-ravenna.t: The da Polenta lordship over the old imperial city of Ravenna, which sheltered Dante in his last years.
lordship-of-ravenna.o: In 1275 Guido da Polenta, called the Elder, took control of Ravenna, ancient capital of the Western Roman Empire and the Byzantine exarchate. His family ruled as lords and later as papal vicars within the Papal States.
lordship-of-ravenna.r: The da Polenta ruled a city whose glory lay in the past, living from the farmland and salt pans of the Romagna coast. Guido's daughter Francesca married into the Malatesta of Rimini and became the tragic heroine of Dante's Inferno. Guido Novello da Polenta welcomed the exiled Dante, who died in Ravenna in 1321 and is buried there. Later members of the family were often violent, and they grew dependent on Venice.
lordship-of-ravenna.e: In 1441 Venice expelled the last lord, Ostasio III da Polenta, and annexed Ravenna to the Republic of Venice. After 1509 the city returned to the Papal States.

league-of-gods-house.t: One of the Three Leagues of the Grisons, formed in 1367 by the bishop of Chur's subjects to stop him handing their land to the Habsburgs.
league-of-gods-house.o: In 1367 the cathedral chapter, the town of Chur and the communes of the Engadine, Bergell and other valleys under the Prince-Bishopric of Chur met to prevent Bishop Peter Gelyto from handing his temporal rule to the Habsburgs. Their pact became the League of God's House (Gotteshausbund), named after the cathedral.
league-of-gods-house.r: The league was a federation of self-governing communes, each with its own courts and assemblies, which sent envoys to a common diet. It allied with the Grey League in 1406 and with the League of the Ten Jurisdictions in 1450, forming the Three Leagues, an associate of the Swiss. The Reformation divided its communes, and much of the Engadine turned Reformed.
league-of-gods-house.e: The league remained part of the Three Leagues until 1799, when French forces attached the Grisons to the Helvetic Republic. In 1803 the Grisons became a Swiss canton, and the old leagues' symbols survive in its coat of arms.

luvale-kingdom.t: A Lunda-derived kingdom of the upper Zambezi whose chiefs grew rich from the 19th-century trade in captives and beeswax before colonial partition.
luvale-kingdom.o: The Luvale (Lovale) trace their ruling line to Lunda emigrants who settled along the upper Zambezi in present-day Angola and Zambia in the 17th century. The senior chief, Kakenge, held ritual primacy over other Luvale chiefs.
luvale-kingdom.r: Luvale chiefs ruled riverine villages of farmers and fishermen, and initiation and masking ceremonies, such as the makishi, were central to social life. In the 19th century Ovimbundu traders and Portuguese-linked merchants from Angola bought slaves, ivory and beeswax, and the Luvale became active raiders and middlemen, often in conflict with Barotseland.
luvale-kingdom.e: In 1905 an arbitration by the King of Italy divided the Luvale lands between Portuguese Angola and British Northern Rhodesia. The Luvale remain a people of both Zambia and Angola, and the makishi masquerade is listed by UNESCO.

livonian-confederation.t: Loose league of the Livonian Order, bishops, nobles and towns of medieval Livonia, bound together by a common diet from 1435 until the Livonian War.
livonian-confederation.o: Terra Mariana had long been divided among quarrelling powers. After the Livonian Order's crushing defeat by Lithuania at Wiłkomierz in 1435, the Order, the archbishop of Riga, the bishops of Dorpat, Ösel-Wiek and Courland, the vassal knighthoods and the towns agreed at Walk (Valga) to settle disputes peacefully and defend one another.
livonian-confederation.r: The confederation had no single ruler or treasury. Its main institution was the Landtag, a diet usually held at Walk or Wolmar, where the territorial lords and estates met to decide on war, peace, coinage and trade. The Livonian Order's master, especially Wolter von Plettenberg, was the leading military figure, and the Hanseatic towns of Riga, Reval and Dorpat had great weight.
livonian-confederation.e: Weakened by the Reformation and internal rivalries, the confederation could not withstand Ivan IV's invasion in 1558. Its members sought protection from Poland-Lithuania, Sweden and Denmark, and in 1561 it dissolved, giving way to the Duchy of Courland and Semigallia, the Duchy of Livonia and the Swedish Duchy of Estonia (1561-1721).

lower-aulaqi-sultanate.t: A coastal sultanate of the Aulaqi tribes, centred on Ahwar on the Arabian Sea, within the British Aden Protectorate.
lower-aulaqi-sultanate.o: The Lower Aulaqi Sultanate, the coastal member of the Aulaqi states, held the plain around Ahwar on the Gulf of Aden. It emerged as a separate polity around 1800, alongside the Upper Aulaqi Sultanate and the Upper Aulaqi Sheikhdom inland.
lower-aulaqi-sultanate.r: The sultans governed farming and fishing communities on the coastal plain and Bedouin in the hills. The sultanate signed protection treaties with Britain and was part of the Aden Protectorate. In the early 1960s it joined the Federation of Arab Emirates of the South, which became the Federation of South Arabia.
lower-aulaqi-sultanate.e: In 1967 the National Liberation Front took control and the sultanate was abolished and incorporated into South Yemen.
